title: AirDrop-style cross-platform file transfer app with radar UI
author: 0xMovez
prompt:
Build "Hop": an AirDrop-style app to send files between a Mac and a Windows PC on the same Wi-Fi. No cloud, no accounts.

Stack: Electron (one codebase for macOS + Windows), plain HTML/CSS/JS UI, no frameworks.

1. Discovery: each device broadcasts a small JSON beacon over UDP (port 47800) every 1.5 s to every subnet broadcast address. Show peers that were seen in the last 10 s. Ignore your own beacons.

2. Transfer: each device runs an HTTP server on a random port. Sender POSTs an offer (file names + sizes), the receiver shows Accept / Decline, then files stream one by one. Support whole folders. Never overwrite: "photo (1).jpg". Reject any path that could escape the download folder.

3. Trust: an "Always accept from this device" checkbox. Save to Downloads/Hop (changeable).

4. Before building any UI, write a Node test where two devices in one process find each other and send a folder + a 3 MB file; compare hashes.

5. UI, Apple-level polish: a radar with this device in the center and peers around it (Apple logo on Macs, Windows logo on PCs). Drag files onto a peer, or click it to pick files. The file chip flies along an arc into the peer, then an iOS 17 NameDrop-style iridescent light wave sweeps across the window (WebGL shader with a Canvas fallback). Progress ring around the peer. Vibrancy on macOS, acrylic on Windows 11. Light / Dark / Auto switch.

6. Icon: macOS squircle, 1024 px, readable at 16 px. Draw 3 concepts, compare them, keep the best.

7. Run independent review passes on the UI and the networking code before shipping.

8. GitHub Actions: on a v* tag build Hop-mac-arm64.dmg, Hop-mac-x64.dmg and Hop-windows-x64.exe and publish a release.

9. Add a startup log and always show the window, so a launch that hangs is easy to debug.

Ship it, then give me the install steps for both machines.

title: Radial aircraft engine cutaway
author: olezhavich
prompt:
Build a 2D animated cutaway of a 9-cylinder radial aircraft engine called "RADIAL NINE" — a clean technical loop that shows how nine pistons share one crankshaft.
STYLE (strict)
Flat 2D technical front view on a deep navy background (#0b1220 or similar), like a premium engineering explainer.
Clean shapes with soft shading, thin light outlines, a subtle hatched pattern on cut metal walls.
Palette: light steel-grey metal; fresh fuel-air mixture in blue; combustion in orange to white; exhaust in smoky grey.
One square composition (1:1), the engine centred and filling ~80% of the square.
NO on-screen UI, no title, no labels by default. The only text is small cylinder numbers 1–9 engraved on the cylinder heads as part of the drawing.
THE ENGINE (must be mechanically correct)
Front view, with the propeller drawn as a faint translucent blur so the engine behind it stays visible.
Nine finned cylinders spaced evenly every 40° around a round crankcase, each cut open to show its piston.
Every cylinder head has an intake and an exhaust valve with rocker arms and pushrods.
A single-throw crankshaft in the centre. One master rod on cylinder 1 is attached directly to the crank pin; the other eight articulated link rods attach to pins on the master rod's big end, not to the crankshaft.
Because of the articulated rods, the pistons' motion is slightly non-uniform. Model the real linkage geometry rather than faking it with identical sine motion.
Four-stroke cycle: each cylinder fires once every two crankshaft revolutions.
Firing order 1-3-5-7-9-2-4-6-8, so the flashes jump around the ring skipping every other cylinder.
THE CYCLE (driven by one crank angle, all motion synchronized)
Intake: the intake valve opens and blue mixture flows in as the piston moves inward.
Compression: both valves closed, the mixture compresses and brightens.
Power: a spark and an orange flame front fill the cylinder and push the piston inward.
Exhaust: the exhaust valve opens and grey exhaust leaves through the exhaust stub.
Rockers and pushrods move in time with their valves.
Gases never pass through solid walls.
ANIMATION (starts on load)
Seamless loop of ~10–12 s at a readable speed (about one crankshaft revolution every 1.5 s), so the firing pattern reads as a spiral of flashes.
A brief 0.5× slow-down once per loop so the articulated rods can be followed.
Subtle heat glow on each cylinder head after it fires, slight engine vibration, the propeller blur spinning in sync with the crankshaft.
KEYBOARD (optional, nothing visible on screen)
Space pauses, S toggles slow motion, L toggles small labels (master rod, link rod, crank pin, intake, exhaust, spark plug), arrow keys change speed.

## 视觉方向
- 风格：工业概念设计图 / 工程设计文档。暖象牙色纸张背景（约 #EDE6D8），炭黑色细线条，克制的强调色：一种信号橙，加一种青色（用于 X-RAY）。不要做成暗色霓虹科幻风。

## 机器人本体（全部程序化生成，不用外部模型）
- 身体由约 40–60 节分段装甲环沿样条曲线排列而成。每节环：圆柱外壳分成多块面板，带程序化细节——通风格栅、舱门、铆钉、凹槽，每节环略有不同。环与环之间是很深的暗色缝隙（见参考图 C）。

## 环境

- 左上参数卡：CLASS、LENGTH 1,312 m、DIAMETER 187 m、MASS、PROPULSION（Peristaltic linear drive）、POWER PLANT、DEPTH CAPABILITY、CREW NONE (AUTONOMOUS)，再加一张迷你部署地图。
- 右上："HEAD SECTION — CROSS VIEW"，用 SVG 绘制（同心环、刀片、刻度环、比例尺），并列出头部各系统。
- 左下：地形示意图，带等高线和沙虫的行进路线，位置标记实时移动。
- 底部一排面板：整条身体的剖面侧视图，标注各模块（tail stabilizer、power & reactor、central actuation、head excavation），配米制比例尺；"SEGMENT DETAIL — TYPICAL RING" 单节环的爆炸图，零件编号；"LOCOMOTION CYCLE" 展示蠕动波的 4 个阶段，与实时动画同步。
- 部件标注在 3D 视图左右两侧排成整齐的两列（Segmented torso rings、Dorsal maintenance hatches、Sand-flow intake vents / Thermal exhaust ports、Modular jaw assembly、Primary excavation ring、Terrain sensor suite），每条标注用细引线连到沙虫身上对应的 3D 锚点；锚点被遮住时标注淡出。

title: Jelly physics simulation improvement comparison
author: vib3coded
prompt:
Create Citrus Jelly — an interactive 3D scene featuring a gummy orange slice. Everything must run directly in the browser in a single HTML file using WebGPU and WGSL shaders. Build genuine volumetric 3D geometry, not an image or a prerecorded animation.
APPEARANCE
A thick semicircular orange slice with vibrant orange flesh, a pale pith layer, and a firmer outer rind.

Visible radial segments, thin internal membranes, and tiny bubbles.
A juicy, translucent gummy material with soft highlights, light refraction, and depth-dependent color.
Avoid making it look like rigid plastic or glass.
Use a light cream background, soft studio lighting, and a contact shadow. Avoid overexposure.
PHYSICS AND INTERACTION

Let users grab any visible point with a mouse or finger and pull it.

Deformation must originate at the grab point and propagate naturally through neighboring areas.
The flesh should stretch and narrow under tension, while the rind offers more resistance.
On release, the slice should spring back gently, with oscillations gradually settling.
Use a stable soft-body simulation: a spring mesh or volumetric elastic constraints with volume preservation.
Segments, membranes, and bubbles must deform with the flesh rather than separating or floating independently.
Include ground collisions: the slice should squash slightly on impact and wobble afterward.
Prevent instant snapping back, endless oscillation, and exploding geometry.
INTERFACE

A minimal editorial layout with generous whitespace.

A large italic serif heading, “Citrus Jelly.”, on the left.
A compact control panel on the right with Firmness and Internal damping sliders.
Give it a nudge, Reset, and Pause buttons.
Show mesh and ¼ speed toggles.
Three color presets: Orange, Blood Orange, and Lemon.
A small interaction hint: “Grab. Stretch. Let go.”
All labels in English, with comfortable desktop and mobile controls.
TECHNICAL REQUIREMENTS

Genuine WebGPU rendering, not a Canvas 2D substitute.

Generate geometry and materials in code without premade models.
Use a fixed simulation timestep and constraints that prevent excessive stretching.
Maintain smooth performance during grabbing, dragging, and release.
Display a clear fallback message when WebGPU is unavailable.
Test different grab locations, strong stretching, oscillation decay, collisions, and reset.
The main priority is a convincing gummy feel. The slice should look soft, juicy, and so satisfying in motion that people want to keep stretching it.

- A square block of translucent jelly sea (≈5.2 × 5.2 units) standing on a paper-studio floor; the camera looks in at the front corner at ~27°. The block's cut faces show candy strata (chocolate bedrock, caramel clay, a shell band, vanilla sand); the sea surface and walls refract and tint what's behind them, with caustics on the sea floor, light shafts, a tinted caustic shadow on the floor, foam lace on the shoreline and a bright meniscus on the cut edges.
- A small tropical island toward the back: sandy beach, a cove facing the viewer, a mossy jungle hump with ~9 gummy palms (ringed caramel trunks, translucent fronds that flutter), lumpy gummy bushes with flowers, ferns, beach grass, rocks around the shore.
- SKULL ROCK at the island's west tip, standing in the shallows: a cartoon skull sculpted as a signed-distance field (cranium, cheekbones, jaws, deep eye sockets, heart-shaped nose, crack on the crown, rock strata and noise, moss on top, a wet band at the waterline), meshed with surface nets; two rows of separate box teeth set into a carved grin. At night its eye sockets glow like a candle-lit cave.
- A PIRATE SHIP riding at anchor in front of the island, seen at three-quarters from the stern: black hull with an ochre gunport strake, red bottom, gunports with cannons, raised quarterdeck with lit stern windows and a stern lantern, three masts (square courses and topsails on fore and main, a gaff sail on the mizzen, a jib to the bowsprit), shrouds and stays, and a Jolly Roger (skull and crossed bones drawn procedurally in the shader) streaming aft. Her anchor chain runs from the bow down through the jelly to an anchor lying on the sea floor.
- The camp on the cove beach: a campfire (stone ring, teepee of logs with glowing ends, embers, a tripod with a pot, two seating logs), an iron-bound treasure chest under a leaning palm with a hinged lid and a heap of gold and gems inside, a shovel in a sand heap, barrels, a crate, a pyramid of round shot, a rum bottle, a rowing boat pulled up with its bow on the sand, and an "X" scored in the sand.
- On the sea floor: the bow half of an old wreck lying on its side with ribs showing and its broken mast beside it, swaying kelp, a few doubloons, bubbles caught in the jelly.

SIMULATION
- Linear shallow-water waves on a staggered grid with a little surface tension (springy jelly); the block can be tipped and the sea sloshes and the jelly wobbles (shear + squash).
- The ship floats on 10 buoyancy points (heave, pitch, roll), is pushed by a gently veering offshore breeze, held by an elastic anchor rode at the bow, and weathervanes into the wind. Her displaced volume is handed back to the sea, so she makes a wake.
- Rigid bodies: cannonballs (dense, fly in a clean arc, punch a crater, sink and roll on the floor), barrels (float on their side), doubloons (flutter down and settle flat). All interact with the sea (buoyancy, drag, splashes, bubbles), the terrain, the skull, the props, the palm trunks and the ship's hull.
- One particle system: fire flames (additive), embers, woodsmoke, muzzle flash, white gunsmoke, sea spray, sand puffs, gold glints over the open chest, fireflies at night.

INTERACTION
- Tap the ship → fire the next gun on the side facing the viewer (ball, flash, smoke, recoil heel). Drag the ship → tow her against the rode; release → she drifts back to her anchor.
- Tap the chest → lid swings open/shut with a bounce; gold glitters. Tap the fire → it roars and throws sparks. Tap the X → three doubloons pop out of the sand.
- Drag across the water to make waves; drag a side of the block to tip it; pick up and throw balls/barrels/coins; drag a palm to bend it; drag empty space or right-drag to orbit; wheel/pinch to zoom.

TIME OF DAY
- A slider from Noon → Afternoon → Golden hour → Sunset → Dusk → Night → Midnight. The sun lowers and warms, the backdrop turns peach, then the moon takes over (dim blue), stars appear on the backdrop, the page UI switches to a dark theme, and the campfire becomes the main light: a flickering point light that warms the sand, palms, sails and gold, reflects in the water, and lights the smoke from below. Stern windows and lantern glow.

UI (editorial, like the series)
- Top-left masthead: eyebrow "MATERIAL STUDIES", big italic serif title "Pirate / Jelly.", a short line of copy.
- Status pill (WebGPU · Live / Paused / Unavailable).
- Right glass panel: "The cove" — buttons Fire a gun / Doubloons / Barrel, a liveliness meter, tally Shots · Afloat · Sunk; "Flavour" — Turquoise, Rum (amber), Kraken (violet) jelly palettes; sliders Firmness, Wave damping, Time of day; Reset / Pause / Reset view.
- Bottom-left "How to play" line plus small instructions. Space fires a gun.
- Mobile: the panel becomes a bottom sheet; touch orbit and pinch zoom.
- Fallback card when WebGPU (or an adapter) isn't available. Respect prefers-reduced-motion.

title: Detailed interactive 3D off-road expedition vehicle in one HTML file
author: maxt3chno
prompt:
You are a senior real-time 3D artist and Three.js engineer. Build a detailed, realistic, interactive off-road expedition vehicle in the existing project using Three.js and WebGL.
Treat the attached image as a visual reference only. It shows a heavily used, boxy vintage 4x4 expedition vehicle: olive-green paint, extensive rust and mud, large knobby tires, a front bull bar and winch, roof-rack cargo, side-mounted equipment, and a rear spare tire. Use the large upper image as the primary appearance reference; use the smaller side and rear views to infer details hidden in the main view. Do not reproduce the image itself as a flat plane, billboard, or texture. Build a real 3D vehicle that looks convincing from every angle.
Required workflow
Work through the phases below in order. At the end of every phase, run or open the project using its existing workflow, inspect the actual result, perform that phase’s checks, fix problems, and repeat the checks until the phase passes. Only then continue to the next phase. Keep the code and project runnable between phases.
Do not mark a phase complete based on code inspection alone when its appearance or behavior needs to be checked in a rendered scene. Do not claim to have verified something you could not inspect. Make routine implementation choices yourself and continue through all phases without waiting for user review.
Phase 0 — Inspect the project and plan the implementation
Inspect the project structure, Three.js version, rendering setup, coding conventions, and available local 3D, image, and audio assets. Identify the existing run and preview workflow. Reuse suitable local assets and existing project patterns where practical. Do not add external dependencies or fetch assets from the internet unless the project already has an established workflow for doing so.
Before modifying files, determine where the reusable vehicle component belongs and how it should be integrated. Then proceed with implementation; do not stop after presenting a plan.
Check before continuing: Confirm that the chosen implementation fits the project’s Three.js version and architecture, that required assets are available or a procedural approach is needed, and that you know how to launch and inspect the result.
Phase 1 — Create the correctly proportioned vehicle body
Build the main 3D silhouette first: a heavy, older utility 4x4 with a tall squared-off body, upright windshield, flat hood, distinct fenders, practical cabin, and visible ground clearance. Establish the wheelbase, cabin, hood, roofline, front and rear overhangs, and overall proportions before adding small details.
Use meters as the approximate unit scale. Target roughly 4.4 m in length, 1.8 m in width, and about 2.2 m tall including roof rack and cargo. Use a consistent local coordinate system: Y is up, X is left/right, and +Z points toward the front. Place the origin at the vehicle’s ground-level center, or document a different origin if project conventions require it.

title: Sound-design pack for a short visual edit
author: AmirMushich
prompt: Build an original SFX palette for my short visual edit in Codex, without a DAW or third-party samples. First map the visual events by function: micro-cut, object lock, texture movement, transition, resolve. Start with only three distinct dry mechanical-digital sounds, not a full pack. Avoid tonal beeps, pitch-sweep lasers, bells, conventional drums and long reverb. Export individual 48 kHz / 24-bit WAVs, a level-matched audition reel and a cue sheet. Check peaks, clean endings and mono compatibility. Don’t claim you can hear the result: ask me which prototype works, which fails and why; iterate from that feedback before making variations.

④GPT6-Astra用プロンプト
_______________________________________＿
あなたは、VTuberの切り抜きやMVを作るモーショングラフィックス担当です。
添付したダンス動画から、VTuberらしい「踊ってみた」風のモーショングラフィックス動画を完成品として書き出してください。

■ 入力
・ダンス動画：添付ファイル（背景は緑、床が黒の場合あり）
・チャンネル名／キャラ名：【例：なし（入れない）】
・締めの一言：【例：よろしくね♡】
・テーマカラー：【例：ピンク・レモン・水色・紺】

■ 絶対に守ること
・画面に出す文字はすべて日本語。英語やアルファベットは一切使わない（「BPM」は「テンポ」、「BEAT」は「拍」、数字は可）
・文字がキャラに隠れて読めなくならないように配置する（文字とキャラを左右に分ける、または文字をキャラより手前に置く）
・流れるコメントはキャラの顔に重ねない

■ 手順
1. 切り抜き
　・緑の強さ（G − max(R,B)）でアルファを作り、縁はなめらかにする。緑かぶりは除去する
　・床が黒い場合は、床のラインより下の暗い部分も透明にする（髪の黒を消さないよう、床より上には適用しない）
　・最大の塊だけ残してゴミを消す
　・最初に数フレームだけ切り抜いてピンク背景に合成し、確認してから全フレームに進む

2. 構成（1920×1080・24fps・元動画と同じ長さ）
　・テンポ128、32拍で場面を切り替える。切り替えは必ず拍の頭にする
　・場面の例：
　　①まもなく開演（線が伸びる）→ ②「踊って」→ ③「みた！」→ ④斜めに流れる文字の帯「リズム／ステップ／キラキラ」
　　→ ⑤集中線の背景で「ビートを」「感じて！」＋絵の具が飛び散る演出 → ⑥縁取り文字の「リズム」と「に、のれ。」＋グリッチ
　　→ ⑦3色の画面にキャラを3人並べる（少し時間をずらす）→ ⑧回るリングと「ダンス」
　　→ ⑨締め「動きで、魅せる。」＋「チャンネル登録」ボタン＋【締めの一言】

3. VTuberらしい演出
　・キャラは白フチ付きのシール風にし、色付きの影か、ピンクとシアンの色ずれを付ける
　・拍ごとに、キャラが少しだけ弾むように拡大する
　・四隅に配信画面風の表示を入れる：「● 配信中」（点滅）、「テンポ128」、「経過 00:00:05:12」、「拍 05／32」、拍のメーター
　・右から左へ流れるコメント（「かわいい！」「８８８８８」「神回きた」「推せる」など）。画面上部に3つの列を決めて流し、同じ列の中で重ならないようにする
　・ハート、キラキラ、水玉模様。場面の切り替えで白く一瞬光らせる
　・フォントは Google Fonts の Dela Gothic One（見出し）、M PLUS Rounded 1c（ボタンなど）、Hachi Maru Pop（コメント）、Zen Maru Gothic（隅の表示）。取得できなければ Noto Sans CJK で代わりにする

4. 音
　・元の音声が曲として使えるか（無音や環境音ばかりでないか）を音量の変化で確かめる
　・使えない場合は、テンポ128のオリジナルBGMを合成する（キック、手拍子、ハイハット、ベース、コード F-G-Em-Am、サビできらきらした分散和音）
　・グリッチ演出の拍に合わせて音も途切れさせる

5. 確認
　・全体を書き出す前に、各場面から1枚ずつ静止画を出して一覧で見る
　・文字が隠れていないか、コメントが顔に重なっていないか、切り抜きの縁が汚れていないかを確かめてから本番を書き出す

6. 書き出し
　・MP4（H.264・yuv420p・AAC）、ファイル名は「踊ってみた_モーショングラフィックス.mp4」
　・最後に、使った音（元の音声か合成BGMか）と、場面の流れを短く報告する

title: Gossip-style vertical video with sourced clips and voiceover
author: dotey

title: Cinematic documentary film about Al Capone with code-drawn frames
author: exploraX_
prompt:
I want a cinematic motion video built entirely from code. No AI video generators and no stock footage. Every frame should be drawn with code (HTML canvas is fine) and rendered to an MP4.

INPUTS (attached):
- Script / voiceover: [attach audio file] -- line timings: [paste each line with its start time, or tell Claude to work them out from the audio]
- Photos of the real people/places/objects: [attached]
- Style references: [attached -- these show the look I want, match their feel]
- Format: [e.g. 21:9, 3840x1646, 30fps] -- length must match the voiceover exactly.

THE STYLE:
- The whole video is ONE continuous camera move over one big world: a map, a desk, a board, whatever fits the story. Nothing cuts and no slides change. The camera glides, pushes in on details, pulls back to travel, and dives in again.
- Motion must feel smooth and filmed. Every start and stop eases in and out. The camera never stops dead: during holds it keeps drifting slowly in the direction it's about to go. Add subtle handheld movement, motion blur on fast moves, film grain, a soft glow and a vignette.
- Real photos and documents drop onto the world as physical objects (prints, papers, clippings), placed where the story happens.

STORYTELLING AND READABILITY RULES (most important):
1. One idea per line of narration. Each line gets ONE hero on screen (a photo, a word or a document) and everything else dims back.
2. Every phrase appears on screen once, never repeated. If the narrator says it, either show it on a real document or type it on screen, never both.
3. No filler text. Body copy on documents should be soft grey lines that read as paper, not words people try to read.
4. Big, readable type: hero words very large, labels never tiny. If someone can't read it on a phone in one second, it's too small or there's too much.
5. Less is more. Leave out decorative clutter (random tape, stamps, memos, extra labels) that isn't part of the story.
6. Visual moments land exactly on the spoken word: a circle drawn as the word is said, a stamp slamming on the beat.

PROCESS:
- Before you build, write a beat table: time → narration → the one hero on screen → any on-screen text. Show it to me and ask me anything that's unclear.
- Take your time. Quality matters more than speed. Prioritise design, smooth movement and clarity over adding more stuff.
- Before the final render, check your own work: look at stills from every beat and frame sequences of the camera moves. Fix anything that's cluttered, hard to read, overlapping, or that jerks or stops abruptly.
- Deliver the final MP4 with my voiceover synced, in the exact format above.

title: Red panda Koda and the giant peach
author: HeyAbhishek
prompt:

Maintain his identical face, amber-brown eyes, cream facial markings, rust-red fur, dark legs, rounded ears, compact proportions and enormous ringed fluffy tail throughout every frame. The reference defines Koda's appearance only.
The entire story takes place on one continuous sunny green mountain hillside surrounded by distant forested mountains. One old peach tree grows from the slope. It has a thick stable trunk, several strong main branches and one thinner flexible outer branch. One enormous ripe golden-orange peach hangs near the end of that thinner branch. A large dense leafy bush grows directly below that side of the tree. A long fallen bamboo pole lies several meters away on the same hillside. Farther downhill, a narrow wooden footbridge crosses a shallow mountain stream. Keep this geography fixed throughout the entire video.
Koda desperately wants the enormous peach. His first idea is simply to climb the tree. He reaches the fruit but moves too far onto the thin outer branch, causing the branch to bend gradually under his weight. He almost touches the peach, loses traction and slides off into the huge soft bush below. Koda refuses to give up. He returns with the long fallen bamboo pole, places it diagonally against a strong fork in the tree and climbs it like a simple ladder. This time he reaches the peach and pulls it free. The peach is far heavier than expected, drops onto the clearly sloping hillside and begins rolling downhill because of gravity. Koda chases it, jumps onto the rolling fruit and accidentally begins riding it. He becomes thrilled and celebrates until he notices a narrow wooden footbridge directly ahead. The peach is much wider than the bridge entrance. It wedges between the entrance posts, stops instantly and Koda's forward momentum sends him harmlessly into a giant pile of dry leaves beside the bridge.
Open at 0:00 with a low wide tracking shot of Koda already sprinting uphill through tall green grass toward the peach tree. His short legs move rapidly and his huge fluffy tail streams naturally behind him. As he reaches the tree, he suddenly looks upward and sees the enormous peach glowing among the leaves. He skids to a stop, stares at it, looks at the trunk and immediately becomes determined.
From 0:02 to 0:05, follow Koda as he rapidly climbs the thick trunk using all four paws. His claws visibly grip the bark while his hind feet push upward. His tail stays naturally attached behind him and reacts only to his body movement. He pulls himself onto a strong main branch and begins moving toward the peach.
From 0:05 to 0:08, show a clear wide side view of Koda carefully stepping from the thick branch onto the thinner outer branch. The peach is just beyond his reach. As Koda moves farther away from the trunk, his weight causes the thin branch to bend downward gradually. The branch does not bend before Koda steps onto it and does not move for any unexplained reason.
From 0:08 to 0:11, Koda slowly stretches one front paw toward the peach. His paw almost reaches it. He leans slightly farther forward and briefly touches the peach's fuzzy surface. He smiles. His rear paws then lose traction on the increasingly sloped branch. Koda freezes, his eyes widen and he begins sliding backward along the branch.
From 0:11 to 0:13, Koda slides completely off the branch and falls directly downward into the large dense bush below. He disappears into the foliage with a huge soft leafy FWUMP. The bush shakes. After a short comedic pause, Koda's head slowly rises from between the leaves. Small leaves cling to his fur. He looks upward toward the peach again and his dazed expression changes into stubborn determination.
From 0:13 to 0:16, Koda jumps from the bush, runs several meters across the same hillside and grabs the end of the long fallen bamboo pole using both front paws. He drags it across the grass toward the peach tree. The bamboo scrapes naturally over the ground. Koda struggles because the pole is much longer than his body, but he never uses or removes his tail as a tool.
From 0:16 to 0:18.5, show the complete setup clearly in one wide shot. Koda positions one end of the bamboo on the grassy ground near the tree. He lifts the other end with both front paws while the grounded end remains in contact with the earth. As Koda walks forward underneath the rising pole, the bamboo rotates upward around its grounded end until the raised end settles securely against a strong fork in the thick tree. The bamboo now forms a stable diagonal climbing pole. Koda steps back, studies it and smiles proudly.
From 0:18.5 to 0:21, Koda climbs the angled bamboo with all four paws. His front paws pull while his hind feet push against the bamboo surface. The bamboo remains stable against the tree. His fluffy tail remains physically connected to his body and trails naturally behind him. He reaches the upper end beside the enormous peach.
From 0:21 to 0:23.5, Koda braces his hind feet against the bamboo and grabs the peach with both front paws. He pulls once and nothing happens. He adjusts his grip and pulls much harder. The short fruit stem stretches under the force. With one final effort the stem breaks with a clear POP. Koda is suddenly holding the enormous peach and gives a huge triumphant smile.
From 0:23.5 to 0:25.5, the peach's weight immediately pulls downward. Koda cannot support it. The peach slips from his paws and drops onto the steep grassy slope below with a heavy THUMP. Because the ground visibly slopes downhill, the peach naturally begins rolling. It starts slowly and then accelerates. Koda quickly descends from the bamboo and runs after it.
From 0:25.5 to 0:27.5, use a dynamic downhill tracking shot. The enormous peach rolls rapidly through the grass. Koda catches up and jumps onto its upper surface. At first he lies belly-first and panics, but after a moment he gets his paws underneath himself and manages to balance on top. His expression changes from fear to pure excitement. He stretches his front paws outward while his huge attached tail streams behind him. Koda begins enjoying the ridiculous ride.
From 0:27.5 to 0:29, track backward in front of the rolling peach. Koda rides proudly with a huge smile while his fur moves in the rushing air. He suddenly looks ahead. His smile disappears. Pull the camera backward enough to reveal the narrow wooden footbridge directly downhill. The entrance is obviously narrower than the giant peach. Koda's eyes widen. He has no time to stop.
From 0:29 to 0:30, show the bridge entrance in a clear wide side view. The rolling peach reaches the two wooden entrance posts and wedges firmly between them with one heavy THUD. The peach stops instantly. Koda's momentum carries him forward off the fruit and into a large soft pile of dry leaves beside the bridge. Leaves burst upward around him. His head immediately rises from the pile, completely unharmed and dazed. One small green peach leaf drifts down and lands gently on top of his head. Koda slowly looks upward with only his eyes. Cut to black.
Use a premium photorealistic 3D CGI animated-feature aesthetic with detailed soft fur, realistic bark, leaves, grass and peach fuzz, cinematic daylight, rich natural colors and expressive physical comedy. Keep the daylight warm and consistent. Use believable gravity, momentum, friction, collisions and character weight beneath the exaggerated comedy.
Koda has exactly one fluffy tail, permanently attached to the base of his spine throughout all 30 seconds. Never detach it, duplicate it, turn it into a prop or place it in Koda's paws. Koda manipulates objects only with his paws and body weight.
The peach remains attached to the same branch until Koda physically pulls it free. The thin branch bends only because Koda moves his weight farther outward. The bamboo moves only because Koda physically drags and raises it. The peach rolls only after falling onto the visibly downhill slope. The peach continuously travels downhill toward the existing bridge. Do not teleport objects, change geography, create duplicate props or introduce unexplained movement.
No humans, no additional animals, no dialogue, no text, no subtitles, no logos and no HUD.
Use playful adventurous orchestral music throughout. Include rapid soft paw footsteps, mountain wind, grass and leaf movement, claw-on-bark sounds, subtle branch creaking, the soft leafy FWUMP of Koda landing in the bush, bamboo scraping over grass, bamboo contact sounds, the fruit-stem POP, heavy peach THUMP, increasing rolling rumble, stronger wind during the downhill ride, an abrupt musical stop when Koda sees the bridge, a heavy THUD when the peach wedges between the posts, a soft POOF when Koda lands in the leaves, brief silence, gentle leaf flutter and one tiny comedic orchestral note when the peach leaf lands on Koda's head.

title: 7.5-second prompt-to-website reveal for a meme-tech landing page
author: notdwd

Ask me for: the product the landing page is for, the prompt a user types, a hero photo for the page, a background photo behind the prompt box, and my model name for the label. Selfie / Smarter, Week by Week"; paragraph "Monke tracks grins, bananas, selfies and naps—then turns every photo into clear, motivating progress you'll actually feel."; CTA "Get the Banana"; features "Grin zones (Z1–Z5 time & trends)", "Banana scores (coach-ready)", "Auto-sync from any camera you steal"; wordmarks BANANA CO. / JUNGLE / OPUS 5.5. <structure>

Use a bold white headline about taking better selfies, a short supporting paragraph, and a clean rounded "Get the Banana" CTA. / Add a minimal top navigation with logo."
f0–29, type: the box starts at x884 y635 709x112 and eases out to x570 y477 778x130 (90% there by f12) while the whole scene pulls back 7%. Typing starts on f4 with a real keystroke rhythm, reaches 30 characters by f26, then stalls. Four white selection handles hug the box corners.
f29–44, charge: a violet solarised wash floods the scene (peak f36). The box tilts back up to 12° (rotateX, peak f36), the handles fly out to the frame corners, and an ASCII field of % @ # ⨸ glyphs appears at the left and right edges. The box grows to a tall card x541–1374, y425→227. On f40–48 the rest of the prompt bursts in (about 50 characters per frame) and fills ~12 lines.
f48–63, settle: the tall card lands at x575 y227 766x626. The camera eases back toward the subject. A black cursor appears on f55 at (1455,595), pointing up-left, and grows to 112 px.
f64–96, press: hard cut to a 3.19x zoom on the send button (75 px becomes 239 px on screen), a pale pink wash across the top. The cursor swings in from the right (f64–68) and glides to the button (f68–80). Press f80–86: the cursor squashes to 0.9, the button inflates 12% and flashes Claude terracotta #D97757, and the box edge bulges under it. f93–96 the frame blurs 6 px under a lavender veil.
f97–120, reveal: wide shot. The page's hero photo zooms slowly behind (1.1% per frame). The box (763x596) drops from y60 to y245 with an ease-out, settled by f110. On f106–110 it turns grey, then goes dark from the bottom while a cyan band sweeps down through it (f111–121), wiping the text away.
f121–145, morph: the box grows into the page, from x576 y245 763x596 to full frame on a fast ease-out (half the distance by f127, full by f145). Its fill is glass: a dark veil at the top, a cyan→white band sweeping down and out, white fading away. Every page element slides from inside the box to its final place on one progress curve (50% at f130, 90% at f147, done at f161). The headline types two lines at once from f122 to f158.
f161–224, pull back: the page shrinks around its centre onto a flat #dddddd background, from 1920 px wide to 1344 px (1634 by f173, 1404 by f190, 1344 by f214). The hero's motion blur strengthens as it goes. f225 is black.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML file, 1920x1080, rendered from seek(t). Every style is a pure function of the frame: no CSS transitions, no timers, no Math.random. Use seeded hashes.
2. Animate with keyframe tables, kf(frame, [[f, value], ...], ease), interpolating numbers or arrays. Every move above is a table of these keyframes.
3. Cut-outs are SVG masks from hand-traced polygons with a 2–3 px Gaussian feather. The motion-blur smear is a scaleX-stretched copy through an SVG horizontal blur (feGaussianBlur stdDeviation="40 0").
4. The press, the grey-to-dark box and the glass card are layered linear gradients whose stop positions are driven by the band value.
5. Sound: no voice.

   - Master to -14 LUFS, true peak -1 dBTP.
6. Render with Playwright, one screenshot per frame, then encode h264 at 30 fps and mux the audio.
</build>

<gotchas>
Measure text only after the fonts load, or the words collide. The cut-out subject must be opaque and crisp; blending it into the sky makes it look like a ghost. The zoom shot is a hard cut, not a zoom animation. Keep the page content inside the card while it grows (overflow hidden), except the nav, which sits above the box early on. Frame 225 is black.

<start>
Ask me for the inputs. Then show me 4 stills (f20 typing, f82 the press, f125 mid-morph, f200 the pull-back) before you render the full film.

<structure>

2. "made for [value]": full-bleed flashes of my best images on 16th notes into the drop, with the line typed over them in white.

7. "Every [output], exactly how you see it": 120 of my images burst from the centre behind a glass caption pill, then collapse into my logo as the name types, with "Out now" underneath. Hold 2s.

<sound>

Duck the music under the voice with a 3-band sidechain (lows 30%, mids 85%, air 55%; 0.3s hold, 50ms look-ahead, 0.5s release), then move each phrase's mids until the voice sits about 9 dB over the music between 300 Hz and 4 kHz.
One downloaded Mixkit SFX per event, placed by its measured peak: a click on every image switch, a key on every typed letter, a soft landing on the stressed word, whooshes, and impacts on the drop and the logo, trimmed around their peak (many are 4 second risers). title: Flat-vector infographic explainer with timed scenes and kinetic text
author: treyscalez
prompt:
<inputs>
Ask me for my topic (a what-if, a "why does X happen", a true story, or how something works), or pitch 3 with one shocking true angle each. Ask which image model I have (GPT Image 2, or another that takes reference images at 4K) and which voice service (ElevenLabs, or Kokoro for free). Then write a 55-65 s script and a shot plan, and show me both before you spend anything.
</inputs>

<direction>
A 1920x1080 flat vector explainer in the style of the big infographic animation channels. Every scene is a full illustrated place (a lab, a street, a classroom, a stage) with characters acting the line out.
Flat colour shapes, no outlines, one slightly darker flat shade for form, a muted palette (dusty blue-grey, slate teal, warm beige, navy, soft purple), salmon-pink skin, big heads, dot eyes.
A new scene every 2-4 s and a hard cut on every sentence that changes the idea. A white splat wipe (0.2 s in, 0.2 s out) between big sections. The camera always drifts 2-4% or pans.
Text lives only on things in the world: signs on posts, hanging boards, chalkboards, building panels and screens.
- It is typed in Montserrat 800 at 26-34 letters a second. Each letter arrives 1.45x big and 0.7 em to the right, then settles in 0.18 s.
- Ink is #2b2d42 on white boards.
- A red X (#d62828, 30 px round strokes, two strokes of 0.11 s each) goes over every wrong idea.
- Every date gets a white 330x120 card top left with an orange #f4a261 calendar.
- Headlines are white 92-96 px caps on a flat colour (#e2552f with drifting lighter puffs, or #5b3fa6 with slowly turning #6a4cb6 gears).
Banned: outlines, motion-design UI floating over the art (code editors, glass cards, checklists), emoji, burned-in subtitles, any channel's logo, a still frame longer than 1 s, and a character who doesn't move.
</direction>

<structure>
Length: the voice decides, 55-65 s at about 190 words per minute.
0 s a second-person hook that flips what the viewer assumes, acted out literally, then a red X on the denial line → 3-8 s the stakes in one shocking true line, with icons popping in one per word → 8-11 s the subject revealed under a spotlight, its name typed on a sign → 11-18 s the origin: the real place with its name typed on its own sign, a date card, people walking in or out of it → 18-24 s the types or parts, landing one by one on their names, each labelled → 24-25.5 s "so how does it work?" as a headline with question marks popping → 25.5-36 s the mechanism acted out in 2-3 places (a chalkboard, a machine, a map), with a counter rolling up to the big number → 36-46 s what it leads to, with characters who react (jump, turn, a "!" pops) → 46-55 s the twist that ties back to the hook → 55 s the last line is a question to the viewer, the viewer character from the hook reacts, and the sign holds to the end.
</structure>

<build>
1. Tools: Python, Playwright with Chromium, FFmpeg, faster-whisper, OpenCV, Pillow, librosa. Install what's missing and tell me what you installed.
2. Art: everything at 3840x2160, with 3-5 frames of the reference channel as style references (crop their logo off first).
   - One EMPTY plate per scene: no people, straight-on, open floor, blank signs and screens to write on in code.
   - Character sheets on solid chroma green #00B140, with nothing green on anyone.
   - Draw any character who gestures a lot WITHOUT ARMS, only round shoulder sockets, so code draws the arms. Draw everyone else in the exact pose their scene needs: side view at a desk, side view walking, seen from behind, sitting.
3. Cutouts:
   - The background is every pixel with G - max(R,B) over 40, within 110 of the median green, connected to the border.
   - Add a 2 px soft alpha band, and clamp G to max(R,B) + 6 inside it.
   - Split heads at the neck, drawing hands, and walkers' legs below the coat hem.
   - Refill each hole with inpainting from the body's own colours (transparent pixels masked too), so a turning piece never shows a gap.
4. Voice:
   - Pick it by measuring median pitch (pyin) and MFCC timbre against a clip of the narrator you want.
   - Generate one take, cut pauses over 0.24 s to 0.16 s, and atempo it to the target length.
   - Get word timestamps with faster-whisper. Every cut, sign and gesture starts on a real word.
5. Film: one HTML canvas where every frame is a pure function of time: window. seek(t), READY, END, and EV with the sound times. One function per shot.
   - Arms: two-bone IK tubes (upper 118, lower 112, 36 thick for a 918 px tall sprite) with mitten hands that open, point or make a fist.
   - Faces blink for 0.14 s every 2.7-4.2 s. Heads nod ±0.035 rad. Drawing hands scribble ±8 px.
   - Walks:
     - Thighs swing ±0.42 rad, and the knee bends 0.75·cos² on the swing.
     - The hips drop so the planted foot stays down.
     - The body moves 1.5 leg lengths per cycle, so feet never slide.
   - Draw each plate inside the same camera transform as everything on it, and clamp the camera to the plate's edges.
   - Things arrive with a spring, a squash or a white puff, never a fade.
6. Render: Playwright Chromium with --allow-file-access-from-files, 60 fps, 6 motion-blur subframes over half a frame, ffmpeg libx264 at CRF 16. Before rendering, show me two 16-frame contact sheets and fix empty boards, overflowing text, covered faces and black edges.
7. Sound:
   - Music: a light curious documentary bed (free on Pixabay), 10-11 dB under the voice in every phrase.
   - SFX: Mixkit, placed by their peaks. A typewriter tick on typed signs, a whoosh on wipes and drops, a pop on signs and icons, a hit on the red X, a ding on ticks.
   - Mix to -14 LUFS.
</build>

<gotchas>
Some image models ignore "no arms"; GPT Image 2 follows it. On outline-free art a floating flood fill leaks into dark clothes, so key by border-connected green instead. Look up repeated words by their occurrence number (the third "and", the fourth "this"), or cuts land on the wrong line; scan the render for single-frame jumps and check that each one is a planned cut. When a scene has a screen or a sign, write on the plate's own blank one (measure its rectangle), never on a card floating over the art.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for my topic, or pitch 3, then show me the script and the shot plan.

title: Interactive translucent gummy-dice playground with soft-body physics
author: vib3coded
prompt:
Create “Jelly Dice” — a polished, interactive 3D playground with translucent gummy dice that users can grab, stretch, poke, and roll. Deliver a complete single-file HTML experience using genuine WebGPU.
ART DIRECTION
Make the dice look like premium gummy candy: rounded corners, glossy surfaces, rich translucent colors, small internal bubbles, and clearly readable pips.
Use a warm off-white background, soft studio lighting, and subtle contact shadows. Keep the composition spacious and elegant, with large dice as the main attraction.
The dice should feel heavy, elastic, and substantial — not weightless balloons, rigid plastic, or liquid slime.
GEOMETRY AND MATERIALS
Generate all geometry procedurally. No external models or image files.
Create rounded cubes with slightly pillowy faces and gently rounded pips.
Use conventional dice numbering, with opposite faces adding up to seven.
Keep pips and internal details attached to the deforming geometry.
Use thickness-dependent translucency, color absorption, refraction, soft internal scattering, and smooth highlights.
Thick regions should have deeper color; thin edges should transmit more light.
Avoid blown-out reflections, harsh black outlines, visible seams, and disappearing surfaces.
Provide six saturated color presets: Emerald, Amethyst, Amber, Sapphire, Ruby, and Lime. Default to Emerald. Changing colors must not reset the simulation.
SOFT-BODY PHYSICS
Use a stable volumetric mass-spring or position-based dynamics system with approximate volume preservation.
Each die must deform locally. Do not fake softness by scaling the entire object.
Pulling a corner or face should stretch that area first, while the rest follows elastically.
Grounded dice should resist immediately tipping over when pulled. Their lower surface should have enough friction to create a convincing anchored stretch.
Stronger, sustained pulls should still lift or overturn them naturally.
Separate rigid-body rotation damping from internal deformation damping, so the dice can feel heavy while remaining visibly squishy.
On release, stretched regions should recoil, wobble, and gradually settle.
Landing should briefly compress the die before a restrained rebound.
Include gravity, inertia, floor friction, and collisions between dice.
Prevent excessive overlap, floor penetration, explosive impulses, and endless bouncing.
Use fixed simulation steps, bounded grab forces, and stretch limits for stability.
INTERACTION
Left-click or touch a die to grab it at the exact contact point.
Drag to stretch, lift, or move it.
A quick tap should produce a small local poke and wobble.
Right-drag or drag empty background to orbit the camera.
Support a limited zoom range and a Reset view button.
Keep object dragging separate from camera gestures.
Offer a selector for 1–5 dice, with three selected initially.
Add a Roll the dice button and Space-key shortcut.
Toss dice with varied trajectories and rotations, then let the simulation settle naturally.

**Collaboration.**

charts,

# 5. THE BIG PERFORMANCE REVEAL

SONNET 5

SONNET 5.5

**10.3% → 70.6%**

10.3%

70.6%

---

# 6. CODING SEQUENCE

This should be one of the hero sequences.

A developer's environment.

Dark terminal.

Code.

Git diff.

Architecture diagrams.

Test results.

Logs.

Multiple windows.

Instead of showing static screenshots, create the feeling of an AI actually working.

Show:

READ

UNDERSTAND

PLAN

EDIT

RUN

TEST

FIX

SHIP

Then accelerate everything.

The camera pushes through the screen.

We transition from terminal → code → architecture → finished application.

**“Understand the codebase.
Make the change.
Check the work.”**

---

# 7. KNOWLEDGE WORK

PDFs

spreadsheets

earnings reports

transcripts

charts

documents

slides

Words.

presentation

documents

images

interfaces

research

design

# 22. PRODUCTION QUALITY

title: 'The First Spark' procedural hand-drawn short
author: morpheusdv
prompt:
PROJECT: THE FIRST SPARK — Procedural Animated Short Film

You are a senior creative coder, generative artist, animation director, and JavaScript graphics engineer.

Your task is to create a visually stunning, fully animated short film using procedural JavaScript drawing.

I have attached a reference image showing a minimalist black-ink animation on an off-white background.

Use the reference to understand the visual language, but create an original animation with its own story, composition, and movement.

Do not create a slideshow, static illustration, or simple particle demo. Build a genuine animated short film with evolving scenes, expressive character animation, cinematic transitions, and continuous visual storytelling.

1. Technical requirements

Build the project using:

JavaScript
HTML5 Canvas 2D
requestAnimationFrame for real-time playback
Procedural geometry and vector-based drawing
Bezier curves, paths, particles, and custom brush strokes
Deterministic animation based on a master timeline

All visual elements must be generated through JavaScript code.

Do not use:

AI image-generation APIs
AI video-generation APIs
External images or pre-rendered video
Stock footage
CSS-only animation
Static illustrations disguised as animation

The animation must be genuinely generated by code.

You may use lightweight JavaScript libraries if they meaningfully improve the animation, but prioritize Canvas 2D.

2. Visual direction

Create a hand-drawn, minimalist, experimental animation.

Visual characteristics:

Warm off-white paper background
Deep black ink illustrations
Slightly imperfect hand-drawn outlines
Organic brush strokes
Variable line thickness
Ink splashes and subtle paper grain
Expressive silhouette-based character design
Fluid, organic movement
Occasional dramatic camera movements
Cinematic composition

The visual result should feel like a professional independent animated short film.

Avoid generic geometric motion graphics, repetitive particle effects, and simple bouncing shapes.

Every scene should have a clear visual purpose.

3. Story: THE FIRST SPARK

Create an original 60-second animated short film.

The story follows a tiny character that emerges from a drop of black ink and gradually discovers how to create a world.

SCENE 1 — THE BEGINNING (0–8 seconds)

An empty off-white canvas.

A tiny black ink droplet appears in the center.

The droplet begins trembling.

Small irregular brush strokes emerge from it.

The ink slowly transforms into a tiny living character.

The character opens its eyes and looks around.

The camera gradually moves closer.

SCENE 2 — DISCOVERY (8–18 seconds)

The character begins walking across the empty world.

Its movement must feel alive, with animated limbs, body deformation, and subtle secondary motion.

Every step leaves behind small ink marks.

The character notices one of these marks and touches it.

The mark begins growing into an organic structure.

SCENE 3 — CREATION (18–32 seconds)

The character discovers that its movements can create new objects.

It draws a line through the air.

The line becomes a tree.

More brush strokes emerge and transform into hills, plants, and abstract structures.

The camera follows the character as the world expands.

Objects must visibly grow and transform through procedural drawing rather than suddenly appearing.

SCENE 4 — CHAOS (32–44 seconds)

The character loses control of its creation.

Black ink spreads rapidly.

The landscape becomes distorted.

Trees twist into abstract shapes.

Ink splashes fill the screen.

The camera shakes subtly as the character runs.

The animation becomes faster and more intense.

Use fluid transitions between all visual elements.

SCENE 5 — THE FIRST SPARK (44–55 seconds)

The character stops running.

Everything becomes still.

A small glowing point appears in its hand.

This is the only moment where a subtle warm accent color may be used.

The character releases the light.

The light expands into a circular wave.

The chaotic ink reorganizes into a beautiful, balanced landscape.

The camera pulls back to reveal the completed world.

SCENE 6 — ENDING (55–60 seconds)

The character stands on a small hill and looks toward the horizon.

The camera slowly moves backward.

The entire landscape gradually transforms into a single small ink drawing on the original empty canvas.

Fade to off-white.

End.

4. Animation quality requirements

This is the most important part of the project.

Every scene must contain actual animation.

The character must have:

Procedurally animated walking and running
Expressive body language
Head and body rotation
Squash and stretch
Anticipation and follow-through
Smooth transitions between poses

Environmental elements must have:

Organic growth animations
Continuous subtle movement
Non-repetitive procedural variation
Smooth transformations between shapes

Implement a virtual camera with:

Position
Zoom
Rotation
Smooth tracking
Cinematic easing

Use layered depth and camera movement to create visual richness.

Do not rely on random movement alone.

The animation should be deliberately choreographed around the story.

5. Timeline and rendering architecture

Create a centralized animation timeline.

Every visual state must be determined by the current timeline position.

Implement a function similar to:

renderFrame(time)

The function must render the correct animation frame for any requested timestamp.

Use seeded randomness so that rendering the same timestamp always produces the same image.

Do not make the animation dependent on the number of previous frames rendered.

This is essential for deterministic video export.

Target specifications:

Resolution: 1920 × 1080

Aspect ratio: 16:9

Frame rate: 30 FPS

Duration: 60 seconds

Provide an option to switch to 1080 × 1920 vertical format for social media.

6. Preview and controls

Create a local web interface that allows me to:

Play and pause the animation
Restart the animation
Scrub through the timeline
Jump between scenes
Adjust playback speed
Switch between horizontal and vertical formats
Preview the animation in real time

Display the current timestamp and scene name.

7. Video export

Implement a reliable video export workflow.

The final animation must be exportable as a high-quality MP4 file.

Use deterministic frame-by-frame rendering to avoid dropped frames or inconsistent timing.

You may use a suitable browser rendering pipeline, a frame-sequence exporter, or FFmpeg.

Do not assume that recording the browser window in real time is sufficient for production-quality export.

Provide a simple export command or interface.

8. Development process

Do not attempt to create the entire film as one enormous, untested code block.

Work in stages.

First:

Create the project architecture.
Implement the Canvas rendering engine.
Implement the deterministic timeline.
Create the character animation system.
Build Scene 1 as a fully functional visual prototype.
Run the project and inspect the visual result.

After the first scene works, continue implementing the remaining scenes.

Test the animation at multiple timestamps.

Check for rendering errors, broken transitions, inconsistent character proportions, and performance problems.

If a scene looks too simplistic, improve its procedural drawing and choreography.

9. Deliverables

Provide:

Complete JavaScript source code
Working local animation preview
Editable scene definitions
Reusable character animation system
Reusable procedural drawing functions
Video export functionality
Instructions for running the project

The final result must be a functioning animation, not just a technical demonstration.

Start by implementing the first scene and the core animation engine. Once the prototype is functional, continue with the remaining scenes.

title: Interactive Lamborghini FL3 tractor diesel engine
author: exploraX_
prompt:
Build an interactive 3D web page: a live "bench study" of the **Lamborghini FL3**, the air-cooled three-cylinder diesel that powered the Lamborghini 2R tractor (1961 to 1967), from the years before Lamborghini built cars. Visitors should be able to start the engine, rev it, load it, cut it open, watch the cooling air, and take it apart. The page should feel like a beautifully printed technical plate that happens to be alive.

## Hard rules

- **Everything procedural.** No 3D models, no Blender, no textures, no image files, no audio files. Geometry, materials, drawings and sound are all generated in code.
- **three.js (WebGL)**, vendored locally, ES modules with an importmap, no build step. It must run from a plain static server.
- **60 fps** on a recent laptop at 1440x900 and on a retina display.
- **Desktop:** the whole sheet fits a 1440x900 viewport with no scrolling.
- **Phone width:** the sheet becomes a vertical scroll with nothing cut off. On touch, horizontal drags turn the engine and vertical swipes scroll the page.
- **No em dashes** anywhere in the copy.

## The engine: facts

Only these figures are published. Use them exactly:

- 3 cylinders, inline, air-cooled, direct-injection diesel, Lamborghini type FL3
- bore 92 mm, stroke 110 mm, 2,193 cc
- 39 hp (29.1 kW) at 2,200 rpm
- electric starter, Bosch injection
- about 2,000 2Rs sold between 1961 and 1967
- factory colours: orange and light blue ("celeste")

The external layout, from photographs of a restored 1962 2R:

- the engine block painted celeste
- an axial cooling blower in a round housing at the front, belt-driven from the crank, with a wire guard
- a sheet-metal air cowl along the cold side
- individual finned cylinder barrels and finned heads, held down by long studs
- a silver inline injection pump on the hot side, with three copper high-pressure lines up to the injectors
- twin fuel filters
- a black vertical exhaust stack with a silencer and a flapper rain cap
- an oil-bath air cleaner
- a dynamo, a starter motor, and a flywheel with a ring gear

Everything else is an assumption and must be labelled **modelled** on the page:

- compression ratio (about 17:1), rod length, valve timing
- idle (about 700 rpm) and high idle (about 2,350 rpm)
- torque curve, friction, airflow, temperatures, fuel use

Never dimension an assumed size in the drawings.

## Art direction: a 1960s Italian two-ink print

It must not look like a Victorian parchment plate or a generic blueprint. Think of a page from an Italian factory manual or a mid-century industrial catalogue, printed in the tractor's own two inks.

- **Paper:** ivory offset stock (about #EEE9DC) with fine paper grain and soft, uneven ink absorption.
- **Inks:** arancio (#E0561C), celeste (#58AED6 for the print, a deeper #3F9DD0 for the painted engine) and near-black (#1C1B19).
- **Type:**
- Bodoni Moda for display: a huge "FL3" with the 3 in arancio, and an italic "Lamborghini" above it.
- Archivo for labels (wide, letter-spaced small caps).
- IBM Plex Mono for numbers.
- Every label carries its Italian term in small italic Bodoni (for example: Hand throttle *acceleratore*).
- **Print details:**
- registration marks in the four corners and a colour bar in the margin
- a thin double frame and a running head across the top: "Bench study · *banco prova*", "Air-cooled diesel · three cylinders · direct injection", "Sheet 03"
- a giant celeste numeral "3" printed faintly behind the engine, slightly out of register
- **Layout at 1440x900:**
- left column: title, deck, lede and the controls
- centre: the 3D engine
- right column: four live instruments
- bottom strip: four live drawings and a readings card

Copy:
- Kicker: "Lamborghini Trattori · 1961–1967"
- Deck: "Three cylinders. No radiator."
- Lede: "Before the supercars, Lamborghini built tractors. The 2R of 1961 carried this engine: 2,193 cc of direct-injection diesel and no radiator, cooled by a belt-driven blower and cast fins. About 2,000 were sold by 1967, and tractor money paid for the move into cars in 1963."

## The 3D model

Build the FL3 to its real proportions: 92 mm bore, 110 mm stroke, cylinders about 150 mm apart, crank axis as the origin.

Exterior parts:

- crankcase with main-bearing ribs and mounting feet, oil sump, timing case, flywheel plate
- three separate finned barrels, with the fins flattened where neighbours meet
- three finned heads with rocker covers and long studs
- blower with a spinning rotor, stator vanes and a guard
- V-belt around the crank, dynamo and blower pulleys
- air cowl with a stencilled "FL3 · raffreddato ad aria"
- intake runners into the oil-bath air cleaner with a glass pre-cleaner bowl
- exhaust manifold, silencer and a flapper cap that lifts on each exhaust pulse at idle
- injection pump with a governor housing whose throttle lever follows the hand throttle
- copper injector lines and a leak-off line, injectors, twin fuel filters
- starter motor whose pinion slides into the ring gear while cranking
- a small name plate reading "MOTORE DIESEL · FL3 · CV 39 · 2200 g/min" (no company logo anywhere)

Moving internals:

- crankshaft with counterweights, pins 120 degrees apart, turning clockwise seen from the blower end
- connecting rods, pistons with rings and a combustion bowl
- camshaft at half speed with lobes timed to the valve events
- tappets, pushrods, rockers, valves and springs that compress, all driven by the same valve-lift curves the simulation uses

Materials and setting:

- **Materials:** glossy celeste enamel with subtle procedural grain, rougher on castings than on sheet metal. Steel, alloy, copper and heat-darkened exhaust.
- **Stand:** the engine sits on an **arancio test stand**.
- **Lighting and floor:** a soft cast shadow and a contact shadow lands on the paper itself (a transparent canvas over the page).
- **Life at rest:** the engine rocks slightly on its mounts against the gas torque.

## The simulation

Write it as a pure, testable module.

- **Kinematics:**
- exact slider-crank piston motion and rod angle
- four-stroke cycle over 720 degrees, firing order 1-2-3, one firing every 240 degrees
- **In-cylinder pressure:**
- polytropic compression and expansion with a double-Wiebe heat release (fast premixed burn plus a slower diffusion burn), tabulated by fuel level
- calibrate the heat release so that full fuel at 2,200 rpm gives exactly 29.1 kW at the flywheel
- peak pressure lands around 70 to 75 bar at full load
- **Crank dynamics:**
- integrate with sub-steps of about 2 degrees of crank, so the instantaneous gas torque gives real speed ripple at idle and real compression pulses while cranking
- flywheel inertia about 0.8 kg·m²
- **Governor and load:**
- an all-speed mechanical governor with about 120 rpm of droop and a little fuel-rack lag
- the hand throttle sets the governed speed between idle and high idle
- the PTO brake applies a load that rises with the square of speed, so 100% load at 2,200 rpm needs exactly full fuel
- **Starting:**
- the starter cranks at about 250 rpm
- the charge needs a few compressions before it lights, the first cycles misfire and burn rich, and that black smoke leaves the stack
- the engine catches in about 1 second and the starter disengages
- **Stopping:**
- friction rises with speed, plus blower drag rising with the square of speed
- an unfired cylinder gives back less than it took to compress (heat lost to the fins), so the engine stops about 2 seconds after the fuel is cut at idle
- **Temperatures:**
- head temperatures come from about a quarter of the fuel's heat going into the metal, removed by blower air that rises with engine speed
- full load settles around 160 to 175 °C
- run thermal time 30 times faster than real time and say so

The simulation emits events with timestamps: crank, fire, misfire, exhaust valve opening, caught, stop, stalled. Events raised between steps (the key) must not be lost.

## Interaction

- **Ignition key:** a round bakelite-and-steel switch. Click (or Space) to start and stop. It shows Start, Cranking or Stop.
- **Two levers:** the hand throttle shows the governed rpm, and the PTO brake shows a percentage. Style them as notched quadrants with orange lever knobs.
- **Four views** (keys 1 to 4), each with a smooth scripted camera move:
- **Painted.**
- **Cutaway:**
- a section plane through the cylinder axes, with cut faces printed as a light arancio hatch
- parts lying wholly in the removed half (pump, filters, exhaust, starter, pushrods, cam) disappear
- pistons, rods and crank stay whole
- a combustion glow fills each chamber as it fires
- **Airflow:**
- everything except the barrels and heads fades to a paper-grey ghost
- barrels and heads show a temperature ramp from deep celeste to arancio
- particles are drawn in through the blower guard, run along the cowl, cross the fins and leave warm on the pump side
- particles are drawn through the metal like the flow arrows of a technical illustration
- **Exploded:**
- waits until the engine has stopped, then separates the parts along sensible axes and holds the crank still
- each part gets a callout: English name in small caps, Italian term in italic, and a leader line to an orange dot
- labels sit on a paper backing and never overlap
- **Other controls:**
- Slow motion (S) eases time to 1/25
- a Sound toggle
- Reset view
- drag to orbit, scroll to zoom
- **Narration line:** a single italic line in the console that reacts to what is happening. Examples:
- "Key turned. The starter pinion meshes with the flywheel and spins the engine at about 250 rpm."
- "Squeezed about 17 to 1, the air gets hot enough to light the diesel. No spark plugs."
- "It caught."
- "Idling near 700 rpm: three power strokes every two turns, one every 240 degrees."
- "The hand throttle sets the governor, which opens the rack until the engine holds that speed."
- "Full PTO load at 2,200 rpm: the rack is wide open and the FL3 makes its rated 39 hp."
- "No water anywhere. The blower pushes air down the cowl, across the fins, and out warm on the pump side."
- "Fuel cut. It runs down and rocks back on its last compression."
- Each view also gets a line of its own.

## Live instruments (Canvas 2D, ink on paper)

1. **Tachometer:** a period Italian dial, 0 to 25 x100 rpm, with an arancio arc above rated speed and an hour meter whose tenths drum rolls.
2. **The cycle:** a 720-degree wheel with three rings (one per cylinder, offset 240 degrees). Power is arancio, exhaust grey, intake celeste, compression hatched. A pointer follows the crank and a dot flashes at each firing.
3. **Indicator diagram:** the live P-V loop for cylinder 1, with the full-load loop dashed for reference, a dot at the current state and the peak pressure labelled.
4. **Chart recorder:** scrolling chart paper with an rpm pen in black and a power pen in arancio.

Below the drawings, a **readings card**:

- live values: speed, power, torque, fuel (l/h), cooling air (m³/min) and head temperature
- marked "live, modelled"
- a footnote listing what is published and stating that the page is an independent study, not affiliated with Lamborghini

Power and torque are measured at the flywheel, so they never overshoot the rated 39 hp during transients.

## Live drawings: blueline prints of the running engine

Front, Right side, Plan and **Section A-A** are real orthographic renders of the same running model, not illustrations. Ink them in a shader like 1960s diazo prints:

- render normals and depth, then draw blue outlines from silhouette, crease and depth edges
- shade with a celeste 45-degree screentone
- print an arancio hatch wherever the section plane cuts metal
- the diazo paper and its faint grid are printed by the shader itself
- add centre lines and numbered cylinders
- Section A-A cuts through cylinder 1 so you see the piston moving. It dimensions only the published bore (Ø 92) and stroke (110), with TDC and BDC lines marked PMS and PMI.

## Sound (Web Audio, synthesised)

- **Exhaust:** each pop is scheduled from the simulation's own exhaust-valve events at the correct sub-frame time. It is not a looped sample.
- **Layers:**
- diesel knock at each injection
- blower roar and a blade-pass tone tracking speed
- valve-gear whirr
- a starter whine that strains on each compression
- a solenoid clunk on start and stop
- the flapper cap ticking at idle
- a soft metallic cue when the engine comes apart and a seating clunk when it goes back together
- **Slow motion** spaces the pops out and deepens them.
- **Mix:** run everything through a compressor. It must never clip.
- **Autoplay:** audio starts on the first user gesture.

## Deliverables

- the page: `index.html`, `css/`, `js/`, with three.js vendored in `vendor/`
- a tiny no-cache static server (`https://serve.py/`)
- a README that separates published facts from modelled ones
- a headless Node check of the simulation that asserts:
- 29.1 kW at 2,200 rpm
- peak pressure 60 to 85 bar
- catches within 3 s
- idles between 650 and 750 rpm
- full load holds about 2,200 rpm and 39 hp
- heads pass 120 °C under load
- it stops after the fuel is cut
- optional: a frame-exact video capture script (virtual time at 60 fps, a drawn cursor with click rings, the sound rendered offline from the simulation's event log so it stays in sync)

## Done means

1. The sheet loads with no console errors and holds 60 fps.
2. Turning the key cranks, catches with a dark puff and settles near 700 rpm.
3. Full throttle plus full PTO load reads about 2,200 rpm and 39 hp, and the P-V loop peaks around 73 bar.
4. Every view works, including Section A-A cutting through the moving piston.
5. The exploded view waits for the engine to stop, and its labels are all readable.
6. Every figure that is not published is labelled as modelled.
7. At 1440x900 nothing overflows, and at phone width nothing is cut off.

title: Stylized anime dungeon fight with slow motion rewind effects
author: aimikoda
prompt:
References:
@[gunslinger ref]: the gunslinger. White hair, wide white hat with a green underbrim, pink halter top, periwinkle-blue off-shoulder jacket, ragged white skirt, green-and-white cowboy boots. Her only gun is one long black revolver, always in her right hand; her hip holster stays empty.
@[giant ref]: the brute. A towering pale lavender giant, small bald head with two red horns, right arm in a black mechanical gauntlet trailing a heavy iron chain, bare massive left arm, ragged pale skirt.

Visual style: Stylized painterly anime matching the reference images: loose flat gouache strokes, blocky color shapes, minimal linework, black ink accents, airy pale off-white light; lavender, periwinkle, sage green and ink black.

Avoid: No subtitles. No BGM. No realistic gore, no blood.

The gunslinger kills the brute with one shot to the back of his head in a pale stone dungeon hall: in slow motion, a rewind, then the same action at full speed. In side views she is at screen left facing screen right and the brute, three times her height, at screen right facing screen left. Sound: dripping water, chain clinks, stone echo. Shot list: 10 shots, about 30 seconds.

Scene 1: Continuous, the dungeon hall.
Shot 1 (0-3s): Wide side shot, low angle, locked-off camera. The gunslinger stands small at screen left, revolver raised; the brute looms at screen right. Cut as he leans forward.
Shot 2 (3-6s): Medium shot on the brute from a low angle at her side; the camera slowly pushes in from his chest to his grinning face.
The brute's line (hungry, amused): "Oh... a crunchy little morsel."
Cut as the line ends.
Shot 3 (6-9s): Close-up under the gunslinger's hat brim, eye level, locked-off camera. One corner of her mouth slowly lifts into a smile. Cut as she drops her weight forward.

Scene 2: Continuous, extreme slow motion. The image turns cooler and desaturated with a soft dark vignette; dust, pebbles and water drops hang almost still in the air; hair and cloth ripple slowly as if underwater; sound sinks to a muffled drone and slow heartbeats. She leaves afterimages: five or six separate see-through copies of her whole body, each frozen in an earlier pose, spaced along her path, edged with a faint cyan and pink fringe; distinct copies, not speed lines.
Shot 4 (9-12s): Low tracking shot at floor level from the side; the camera slowly travels left to right with her. The gunslinger slides feet-first on her hip toward the brute, pebbles kicked up and floating beside her, a row of afterimage copies behind her. His fist slowly descends toward where she stood. Cut as she slides between his planted legs.
Shot 5 (12-15s): Low angle from behind the brute, his face hidden; the camera slowly tilts up his back. The gunslinger slides out from between his legs toward the lens, springs up and turns to face his back, afterimages stacked along her rising path, until she floats level with the back of his head, her back to the camera, revolver aimed at his nape.

title: Interactive 3D fluffy watermelon you can rotate and zoom in browser
author: vib3coded
prompt:
Build a single self-contained HTML page (no build step) showing an interactive 3D "Fluffy Watermelon" covered in long fur, rendered with WebGL using three.js r147 (UMD build: https://t.co/e5eRvHwZc8). All UI text in English.

SCENE & LOOK
- Full-screen canvas on a soft watermelon-flesh pink studio background: vertical gradient #ECB3AB → #F7CFC7 (lighter band in the middle) → #E8A9A0, used as the scene background.
- A big oblong watermelon lying on its side along the X axis: half-length 1.38, radius 0.98, blunt barrel-like ends, small dimples at both ends, slightly flattened belly, subtle surface unevenness. Start in a 3/4 view (about -0.32 rad around Y, 0.1 rad tilt), camera FOV 30°, framed to fill ~80% of the height.
- Rind pattern under the fur: light green (#A8D66B) with 16 dark green (#1C4D1C) stripes running stem to blossom, with ragged finger-like edges (sine meander + value noise), plus a pale cream "field spot" on the underside. Each hair takes the colour of its own root, so the stripes stay crisp through the fur.
- A short, dried, ribbed stem stub at one end with a slightly domed pale cut cap, and a thin curly helical tendril springing from beside it.
- One directional light from upper-left-front, wrap diffuse, Kajiya-Kay anisotropic highlight along the hair tangent, darker roots (occlusion by hair height), slight per-hair brightness variation.

FUR (most important: it must look crisp, never blurry)
- Fur length 0.2 units. Hairs grow out along the normal, then bend: combed from the stem end toward the blossom end and draped down the flanks (no whorls at the ends), plus slight gravity.
- Undercoat: shell texturing with ~64 instanced shells of the body mesh that reach only 50% of the fur length. Procedural hair cells in UV space (density scaled so one cell is ~3.4 device pixels at the default view), two hair populations (long + fine underfur), hairs gathering into locks toward their tips, analytic anti-aliased coverage, alpha blending, shells write depth. Fade shells out where the surface is seen edge-on and discard faint fragments, so no dotted rim appears at the outline.
- Guard hairs: ~90,000 individual tapered, camera-facing ribbon strands (instanced, 7 segments each) that follow exactly the same bend function, with a minimum width of ~0.75 px so they stay sharp. Draw them twice: once before the shells and once after (depth-tested), so faint edge fur never hides them and they always lie crisply on top.
- Always render at the device's full pixel ratio (capped at 2) and NEVER lower it for performance. If frames are slow, reduce the shell count first (down to 32), then the guard-hair count.

INTERACTION
- Drag to rotate freely (trackball style) with inertia after a flick. The fur lags behind the rotation through a damped spring and flops back. Gentle idle breeze in the fur; after 3 s without input, a slow auto-turn.
- Mouse wheel / pinch to zoom (smooth dolly). Double-click or "0" resets with an eased animation. Arrow keys rotate.

title: High-energy manga-style AMV edit with split-panel motion graphics
author: aimikoda
prompt:
Create a high-energy 16:9 music video using both supplied video clips, edited to exactly match the full duration of the supplied music.

EDITING:
Analyze both clips and the soundtrack. Select the strongest moments, creatively cut, interleave, rearrange and combine footage from both sources. Build a cohesive, fast-paced edit driven by the music's rhythm, energy, transitions and emotional progression. Freely alternate between clips, create visual connections and synchronize key actions with musical accents. Avoid simply playing the clips sequentially.

GRID STRUCTURE:
Use a dynamic, asymmetrical manga-inspired panel layout with large dominant panels, narrow strips, tilted rectangles and smaller supporting panels separated by clean white gutters. Use the reference image strictly for panel geometry, not its artwork or visual style. Mix moments from both clips across different panels, creating coordinated compositions. title: Pixel-art tennis club diorama on a floating island

prompt:
Make a pixel-art 3D diorama of a small tennis club on a floating island, the same series and engine as my other pixel dioramas (three.js, orthographic isometric camera turned in quarter steps, a small render target with no anti-aliasing snapped to whole pixels, depth-based outlines, a fixed 64-colour palette matched in OKLab, hard sun shadows, day/dusk/night, rain with puddle reflections). The club: one court inside a chain-link fence with low dark-green windscreens reading LOVE ALL, a net that sags from 1.07 m at the posts to 0.914 m at the strap, the umpire's high chair with a sunshade and the players' chairs with parasols, a three-row stand, a clubhouse with a red roof, a clock showing the real time, a flag and a terrace, a groundsman's shed, floodlights (spotlights aimed at the court, so night stays dark around it), poplars and a gravel path. title: Pixel-art basketball court diorama with weather
author: vib3coded
prompt:
Build "Corner Court" — a single-file, real-time three.js (r160, ES module via import map from jsDelivr) page: an isometric diorama of an original street basketball half court on a floating city block, rendered as crisp pixel art. UI text in English.

RENDER PIPELINE
- Orthographic camera at ~31° elevation, azimuth 45° + 90° steps (animated; drag sideways or buttons), wheel/pinch zoom; fit the whole slab into the free screen area.
- Render into a small target (screen / pixel size) with no anti-aliasing; snap the camera to whole pixels.
- Post pass:
- depth outlines (darken a pixel >0.55 m in front of a neighbour);
- nearest colour of a fixed ~54-colour city palette in OKLab (concrete/asphalt greys, sky and night blues, court teal, terracotta/orange, reds, yellows, leaf greens, skin/wood, dusk purples, neon pink); optional 4×4 Bayer dither;
- whole-pixel upscale via texelFetch; the background (depth = 1) is the page colour.
- Hard shadows (BasicShadowMap); flat-shaded Lambert low-poly.
- Puddle reflections: render the scene mirrored about the ground (scene.scale.y = -1, ground meshes and rain hidden) into a second target, sampled at gl_FragCoord in the ground shader.
- "Raw 3D" mode: the same scene at full resolution with MSAA.

SCENE
- A ragged-edged slab: grass over soil over rock.
- An asphalt pad painted texel-by-texel at 10 px/m: teal inside the 6 m arc (straight corner lines), terracotta key, white lines, free-throw and restricted circles, cracks, worn paint, a stencilled "COURT 7".
- Hoop: padded navy pole, arm, backboard with its square, orange torus rim, and a line-segment net that sways when the ball goes through.
- Chain-link fence behind the hoop (alpha-tested diamond texture).
- A brick corner shop with an awning, lit windows, a pink "OPEN" neon sign and a vending machine.
- A long wall with an original sunset-city mural.
- A sidewalk with a bench and two seated spectators.
- Floodlights, a streetlight, low-poly trees, hedges, a dumpster, a fountain, a bike rack with two bikes, a hydrant.
- Pigeons that peck and fly off when players or the ball come near.

PLAYERS — procedural rigs of ~17 boxes
- Two-bone IK for legs (running stride, defensive slide, tucked jumps) and arms: dribble hand following the ball, jump-shot set point with release and gooseneck follow-through, layup reach, two-hand dunk, chest pass, rebound/contest reach, celebration.
- Spectators sit, cheer on makes and open umbrellas in the rain.

GAME — streetball 2v2 half court
- Make it take it; 1s inside the arc, 2s beyond; first to 11; win counter.
- Check ball at the top (pass to the defender and back). A change of possession must be cleared beyond the arc.
- Offence AI: dribble to spots, drive when the lane is open, pull-up jumpers when open, layups/dunks at the rim, passes when pressured; the off-ball player spots up or cuts. Man-to-man defence with stance, gap control, steals and contested jumps (blocks).
- Ball physics with substeps: bounces on asphalt, sphere vs torus rim and backboard box, net drag, pole, fences, wall, slab edge.
- Jumpers aimed on a ballistic arc (~50°) with speed/aim noise growing with distance and contest.
- Layups lofted to a peak above the rim so they drop in.
- Rebounds with jumps; out of bounds goes to the other team.
- Score, possession and status messages ("SWISH", "BLOCKED!", "TAKE IT BACK", …) on a lit scoreboard.
- Clicks: the ball handler shoots, his teammate gets a pass, the court sends the handler there. Shoot/Pass buttons.

WEATHER AND TIME
- Day / Dusk / Night lighting presets blended over ~1.6 s; floodlights, streetlight, neon and windows at night.
- Dry / Drizzle / Downpour: rain as short line streaks with splashes. A wetness value rises and slowly dries: the asphalt darkens, puddles spread from low spots in a precomputed depth map and mirror the scene, rain rings flicker in them; feet and the ball splash.

UI
- Pixel display font (Silkscreen) and a clean body font; light/dark themes via tokens.
- Controls: Time, Weather (with a court wetness bar), Shoot, Pass, New game, Pause, Turn left/right, Pixel art/Raw 3D, Pixel size, Palette/Dither/Outlines.
- A "How it's drawn" panel; a stacked mobile layout with no horizontal scroll.
