title: Home network control demo with Claude Code

prompt:
These are my own devices on my home network, but I don't know their brands and models.

Find the devices on my own network: reach every address in my own subnet once (one ping each; ask me first if the subnet has more than 256 addresses), then read the ARP table, then mDNS (Bonjour) and SSDP (UPnP), then the router's client list if I've given you its login. If a VPN is on, ask me to pause it. Ask me whether I also have a guest or IoT network. For each device, tell me what it is, with brand and model where you can, and how sure you are. If only a chip maker shows (Espressif, Tuya and the like), ask me what that device is.
Then list what you found and ask me which devices I also have that aren't on the network (an IR-only AC, a fridge, a microwave and the like); for those, offer the next best option (an IR blaster, a Wi-Fi sensor).
Then ask me which ones to make mine, and for each one I pick, make it mine: control from this chat, and fix what bugs me. If I say "just diagnose", change nothing.

Rules for every device
- Only my own devices on my own network. If this computer isn't on my home network (a cloud session, a virtual machine, or WSL without mirrored networking), say so and stop. To find them: reach every address in my own subnet once (one ping each; ask me first if the subnet has more than 256 addresses), then read the ARP table (a device that ignores ping still shows up there); then mDNS (Bonjour) and SSDP (UPnP); then the router's client list if I've given you its login. If a VPN is on, ask me to pause it: it can hide my home network. Ask me whether I also have a guest or IoT network. Never scan or touch any other network.
- On macOS, if pings or connections to my devices fail with "No route to host", tell me to allow this app under System Settings > Privacy & Security > Local Network, then retry.
- One device at a time, in the order listed (or the order I pick), with the router's Wi-Fi changes last. Finish it, or tell me it's stuck, before the next.
- Back up first: save each device's current settings in its own folder under "rea-home-devices" in my home folder before any change. Keep that folder private: it can hold passwords and tokens, never share or upload it. Keep README.md and CLAUDE.md there listing every tool you made and how to run it, so a new chat started in that folder can use them.
- Before each change, show the old and new value and wait for my yes. Read the value back after. Keep a way to undo every change.
- Build each device's limits below into its tool's code too, so a later request can't break them.

- Roll out: the hangar door lifts, the erector carries the rocket out horizontally on rails and stands it on the mount; it vents LOX wisps.
- Launch: 10-second count with beeps and the clock, strongback leans back, deluge water, ignition at T−3 with huge steam clouds boiling out of the trench toward the sea, slow liftoff, the block trembles, the crowd cheers, gulls go up. The rocket pitches downrange and climbs out of sight leaving a billowing exhaust trail; the camera rises with it.
- Staging: MECO, separation, the upper stage lights a pale blue-violet vacuum flame and leaves. The booster flips, boostback burn, grid fins out, entry burn, steers down, landing burn on one engine, legs swing out, touchdown — on the drone ship or back at the landing zone (toggle, or tap the ship / the pad). Double sonic boom (triple for the landing zone). Boosters come back sooty; the deck and pad get scorched.
- Recovery: the tug tows the drone ship to the quay; the crane hooks the booster, lifts it (pendulum swing), folds its legs, sets it on a stand; the ship is towed back out. Fairing halves come down under orange-and-white parafoils, circling in: one lands in the boat's net, the other splashes and is fished out; the boat brings them home.
- Reuse: the next rollout takes a flight-proven booster ("B1 · flight 2", soot partly cleaned).
- Storm: wind, waves, rain, darkened room, lightning on the masts, the crane or the sea. No launches in a storm or above 15 m/s ("No go · weather / wind"); a count in progress holds.

LIFE
- Brown pelicans that circle and plunge-dive for fish, gulls on masts, lamps and roofs, a pod of bottlenose dolphins, manatees grazing the shallows and surfacing to breathe, fish schools, moon jellies; pad crew who leave before the count, hands on the quay, spectators who raise their arms at liftoff and landing.

RENDERING
- Engine plumes as glowing translucent cones (white-hot core, orange, shock diamonds low down, widening and turning blue-violet in thin air) that light the ground, the smoke and the rocket orange; steam and exhaust as soft lit puffs; soot streaks on flown boosters; shadows, refraction, caustics.

CONTROLS & UI
- Buttons: Roll out, Launch (Hold during the count), Land on ship / Land at pad, Storm. Space rolls out / launches. Taps: rocket = launch, hangar = roll out, drone ship / landing zone = choose landing site.
- Tallies: Launches, Landings, Fairings; status lines for the Rocket (T−/T+ timeline: Liftoff, Max Q, Stage separation, Boostback, Entry burn, Landing burn…), the Drone ship and the Fairing boat.
- Flavours: Lime, Curaçao, Blackcurrant. Sound toggle, pause, reset, view.
- All sounds synthesised with WebAudio, only for events (door motor, hydraulics, countdown beeps, engine roar loop while burning, sonic booms, touchdown thud, tug horn, winch, net catch, thunder) — no background ambience.
- Mobile bottom sheet, touch orbit, pinch zoom; a fallback message without WebGPU.
- Copy: "Launch Jelly. A spaceport on a low island, its rockets flying and coming home, set in a block of jelly." — "Roll it out. Light it up. Bring the booster home."

title: 20-second kinetic identity bumper
author: techhalla
prompt:
You are a world-class motion designer doing a 20.00s kinetic identity bumper for TechHalla — an AI creator known for stealable workflows, not vibes. This piece must feel like the best designer in the room made a street-poster that moves. Showreel stakes: if this is weak, you don’t get hired.

DURATION: exactly 20.00 seconds. LOOPABLE: frame 0 == frame last (position, opacity, cursor if any).
FORMAT: one HTML file, 1080×1080 (square, X-native). 60fps.
PALETTE (strict):
- bg # 0A0A0A
- magenta # FF2BD6
- acid green # B8FF00
- white # F5F5F5 only for primary readable type when needed
No other hues. No gradients on UI chrome. Magenta/green may misregister (print offset) by 2–4px on impact frames only.

TYPE SYSTEM (use all three; never one font for everything):
1) Display / scream: Archivo Black (or equivalent ultra-condensed black) — 1–4 words max
2) Urban grotesque: Syne ExtraBold — secondary hits, stacked lines
3) Mono / “prompt code”: IBM Plex Mono Medium — small labels, timestamps, fake prompt crumbs
Tracking: display −40 to −80; mono +20. Optical kerning. No cute script fonts.

MESSAGE (locked — do not soften, do not add filler slogans):
Beat hits in this exact order:
1. STOP SCROLLING
2. AI VIDEO ISN’T EXPENSIVE
3. BAD PROMPTING IS
4. WORKFLOWS > WISHES
5. STEAL THE PROMPT
6. @ TECHHALLA
Supporting crumbs (mono, ≤18 chars, never full sentences): JSON · H3 · SEEDANCE · 0 KEYFRAMES · MAGNIFIC · COPY/PASTE

NARRATIVE ARC (20s):
0.0–2.5s  COLD OPEN — “STOP SCROLLING” slams in from below with spring overshoot; magenta smear trail; acid green baseline ticks across like a waveform.
2.5–6.5s  THESIS A — “AI VIDEO ISN’T EXPENSIVE” locks to a poster grid (baseline grid 8px). Letters scramble (seeded Fisher–Yates per glyph) then snap on the beat.
6.5–10.5s THESIS B — “BAD PROMPTING IS” replaces it via mask wipe through the letterforms (the outgoing line is the mask). Magenta/green channel split on the cut.
10.5–14.5s PROOF FLASH — rapid kinetic stack: WORKFLOWS > WISHES, then mono crumbs orbit a central block like a terminal. One fake “prompt block” types 3 lines max, then gets crossed by an acid green strikethrough that becomes a underline for STEAL THE PROMPT.
14.5–17.5s BRAND LOCK — @ TECHHALLA centers; display weight. A thick magenta bar and a thin acid green rule form an L-bracket mark (custom, not a logo download).
17.5–20.0s SETTLE / LOOP — hold lockup; micro-breath (scale 1.000→1.012→1.000); last frame == first ready for loop.

CONCRETE TECHNIQUES (required — implement, don’t approximate):
1. seek(t) pure function of time. No CSS transitions. No setInterval. No React state across frames.
2. Springs = closed-form step responses. Stack one spring per target change so motion stays deterministic.
3. Kinetic type: per-glyph spring (y, opacity, blur). Stagger = 1/16 note at 120 BPM (125ms).
4. Print misregistration: on accent frames only, duplicate text layer offset (±2–4px) in magenta and acid green at 40% opacity.
5. Mask reveal: destination text revealed by animating a path mask derived from the outgoing word’s outlines.
6. Camera: one orthographic camera; only punch-in (1.0→1.08) and horizontal smash-pans timed to beats — never random drift.
7. Motion blur: render 4 subframes per frame, blend (tmix-style).
8. Beat grid: 120 BPM, downbeat at t=0. Something must land on every beat for the first 16 beats; after that, every other beat is ok.
9. Pre-pass: before full render, export one still per major beat (8 frames). Fix cramped type, orphan words, low contrast — then render.

BANNED:
Generic AI clichés (brains, robots, neural nets, sparkles), soft gradients, bouncy cartoon easing, particle explosions, stock “futuristic HUD”, long paragraphs, narrator essay energy, Canva-deck energy, extra slogans beyond the locked message, purple/blue neon, glassmorphism.

If Astra already blew our minds… Opus 5.5 is a monster 😱

title: Opus delegates to Haiku: watercolour character motion short
author: kelanoo
prompt:
You're directing a 20-second animated short about the Claude Haiku 5.5 release. You're the director, the art department, the animator, the sound designer and the QA team, and you have real tools to call.

I'm giving you the idea, the tools and the quality bar. Everything else, from the beats to the look to the jokes, is yours to design. I trust your taste more than a beat sheet I could write. Your capabilities are far beyond what you assume, so work like it: plan carefully, push the craft, and use the tools and the time this deserves. Spend generously where it improves the film and economically everywhere else.

Final output: `out/level3.mp4`, 1920×1080, 30fps, exactly 20.0 seconds, with voices, music and sound design. At the end, you'll also save your process as a reusable skill.

---

## 1. The idea

**Opus is overloaded with work it shouldn't be doing.** It's buried in small, repetitive tasks: summaries, classifications, lookups, compactions. Then it has a realization: it can hand all of that to Haiku. It calls Haiku, Haiku arrives fast and clears the pile, and Opus is finally free to do the hard, important work it's built for.

That's the premise. How you tell it is up to you: the staging, gags, rhythm, camera, character beats, what the eureka moment looks like, how Haiku arrives, and how the delegation plays out. Sonnet can appear if it earns its place.

**Fixed points:**
- 20.0 seconds, 16:9.
- Opus and Haiku are characters in the same family as the Claude character.
- The film must read with the sound off.
- The ending respects reality: Haiku takes the volume, and Opus keeps the hard thinking. Anthropic says Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 remain the better choice for complex agentic coding, so Haiku is never shown replacing Opus.

---

## 2. Style reference

The reference is Jake Moran's "Animated agent session story": 
https://
prompt-motion.com/jake11moran-a2
69c4
…. It was made with this skill: 
https://
github.com/heygen-com/hyp
erframes-community-skills/tree/master/skills/session-story
…. Read the skill, including its references on motion and the room.

Take from it:
- The hand-drawn watercolour-on-paper look.
- A cozy room as a world.
- Cartoon blocks with faces as characters.
- Physical paper props that carry the story (paper planes as tasks).
- A score that's cued to every action.

Don't copy it. Use it as a starting point and push it further: richer staging, better acting from the characters, more cinematic camera, and a stronger hook. It should look like it belongs to the same family, made by someone who studied it closely.

---

## 3. Facts (lock these before any creative work)

Fetch 
https://
anthropic.com/claude-haiku-5
-5
… and write `facts.json`: every claim you might use, each with the exact supporting sentence from the page. Only claims in `facts.json` may appear on screen or in dialogue.

This is a story first, so use one or two facts at most, woven into the world rather than presented as slides. For example, a price tag being re-stamped, or Haiku's speed shown rather than stated. The film must end on a card with **Claude Haiku 5.5**.

---

## 4. Audience and hook

The audience is AI and developer Twitter/X: people who use Claude every day and know the model names and the jokes about them. Before writing the treatment:
- **Research:** spend a little time on how people currently talk about Opus, Sonnet and Haiku, and what's being said about this launch. Find one or two references or running jokes this audience would recognize and enjoy. Use them only if they fit the story naturally. Never use real people or brand logos.
- **The hook:** the first second has to work as a still frame on a busy timeline. Someone scrolling should instantly see "a character drowning in work" and want to see what happens.
- **Text on screen:** this is motion design that tells a story, not a lyric video. Use text sparingly and only where it adds something: a beat the picture can't carry alone, the fact stamp, and the end card. Integrate it into the world (painted, stamped, written in marker) rather than overlaying it.

---

## 5. Tools

The keys are in `.env`. Pick the best tool for each job, and tell me which you chose and why.

| Tool | Key | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| Web search and fetch | — | Source page, style reference, audience research |
| Higgsfield (connector) | — | Image generation; call `models_explore` first to pick the best model for flat illustrated characters. Also music or sound effects if its audio models are the best fit. |
| GPT Image (OpenAI) | `OPENAI_API_KEY` | A second image model. Test both on the same prompt and keep whichever matches the style better. |
| ElevenLabs | `ELEVENLABS_API_KEY` | Character voices, sound effects, and music (Eleven Music) |
| Remotion | — | The film itself |
| ffmpeg + Python | — | Audio analysis, frame extraction, checks |
| Subagents | — | Parallel research and independent review |

---

## 6. Order of work

### Step 1: Treatment
Write `treatment.md`:
- Your take on the story in one paragraph.
- The beat sheet with timings.
- What happens in each shot: camera, acting, the gag.
- Where the music hits.
- What each character says.
- Which fact appears and how.
- Why this version is the strongest way to tell it.

Write two or three distinct treatments, then pick one and explain why.

### Step 2: Style bible
Write `style/bible.md`:
- Palette: 6 colours maximum, with hex values and a reason for each.
- Ink line rules: weight, and the "boiling" redraw jitter.
- Watercolour and paper texture.
- Lighting.
- Type: local font files only.
- Character design rules for Opus and Haiku: size ratio, shapes, how each one moves, and their expression set.

### Step 3: Key art (images as the base, no video generation)
The generated images are your key frames and design references. You are the in-betweener. Generate:
1. **Style frames:** 3 options of the world. Pick one.
2. **Character sheets:** Opus and Haiku, each with front, three-quarter and side views and their full expression set. Use the chosen style frame as a reference so everything shares one world.
3. **Key poses:** one image per key pose in your treatment (roughly 6–10), each built from the character sheets and the style frame, matching the camera and composition of the shot.

Put everything on one contact sheet.

**Stop and wait for my approval** before building anything.

The images are references. The final film is drawn in code to match them, and generated images never appear on screen. Trace the shapes, poses, proportions and composition from the key art into SVG, and animate between them.

### Step 4: Audio first
The film's timing comes from the audio.
1. **Voices:** audition at least 2 ElevenLabs voices per character. Opus should feel warm, low and deliberate. Haiku should feel quick, bright and eager. Generate each line separately, with 2 takes, and keep the best delivery.
2. **Music:** generate a track that fits your treatment, about 22s long, with its structure matching your beats: for example, a drop when Haiku arrives. If the generated track won't land on your beats, trim and offset it with ffmpeg rather than changing the picture.
3. **Sound effects:** a sound for every physical action. Paper, whooshes, impacts, the lightbulb, stamps.
4. **Timing map:** detect the music's beat onsets and write `timing.json`. It holds every beat time, the drop frame, each voice line's start and end frames, and every key action snapped to the nearest beat. All animation timing reads from `timing.json`, with nothing hardcoded.
5. Play me the audio-only mix before building the picture.

### Step 5: Build in Remotion
- **Components:** one per character, prop and set piece. Story beats live as data in `story.json`.
- **Drawing:** watercolour fills via SVG turbulence and displacement filters, a multiply-blended paper texture, and boiling ink lines.
- **Motion craft:** anticipation before every big action, follow-through after, squash and stretch, springs for landings, arcs for every moving object, and no linear easing.
- **Acting:** the characters have to perform. Give them readable poses, holds where the audience needs to read a face, and timing that's funny.
- **Mouths:** mouth shapes driven by the voice track's loudness. They must be still when the character is silent.
- **Camera:** push-ins, a whip or a shake where it helps. Motivate every camera move.
- **Mix:** music, voices and sound effects on separate layers. Duck the music under dialogue.

---

## 7. Verification loops (do not skip any)

1. **Key-pose match:** at every key pose, render the frame and compare it side by side with its key art. Write what differs and fix it.
2. **Sound-off read:** render a silent cut. A fresh subagent that has seen nothing else reviews a contact sheet at 2 frames per second and retells the story. If it can't, the staging failed. Fix it and repeat.
3. **Sync check:** list every catch, landing, stamp and dialogue line with its actual frame vs its `timing.json` target. Everything must be within 1 frame.
4. **Fact check:** every word on screen and in dialogue, matched to `facts.json`. Cut anything unmatched.
5. **Technical:** duration exactly 20.0s, stereo audio, peaks below −1 dBFS, no unintended dead air.
6. **Director's review:**
   - Watch the whole film at least twice as frames.
   - Write a brutal critique as the most demanding motion designer you know: what feels assembled, what's slow, what doesn't land.
   - Fix the top 3 issues, then review again.
   - Only then hand it over, with a 10-frame contact sheet.

---

## 8. Package it as a skill

Save the full pipeline as `.claude/skills/launch-film/SKILL.md`, so that next time *"Make a launch film for [URL] about [idea]"* is enough.

The skill should include:
- The fact lock
- The treatment process
- The style bible as a reference file
- The key-art process with both image models
- Voice auditions
- Music and sound effects
- The timing map
- The reusable Remotion components
- Every verification loop

---

## Approval gates
1. `facts.json` and the chosen treatment
2. Style bible, character sheets and key poses → **wait for my approval**
3. Audio-only mix and `timing.json`
4. Final film, contact sheet and critique
5. Skill

Keep a task list throughout. At each gate, show me the work, not a description of it.

title: Browser-based jelly watermelon you can cut into pieces
author: vib3coded
prompt:
Build "Whole Melon": a single self-contained HTML file (all JS/CSS inline, no build step, no libraries) with a big whole watermelon made of glossy jelly that you can grab, wobble and cut into pieces with a knife. Render with raw WebGPU (WGSL); if WebGPU is missing, show a clean fallback card.

SHAPE AND MATERIAL
- The melon is a signed distance field: an ellipsoid (~32 cm long) lying on its side with a softly flattened belly.
- Layers by depth under the skin: dark-green skin with irregular darker stripes running pole to pole (seamless all the way around), a pale pith band, then translucent red flesh that brightens toward the rind. Add a pale yellow field spot on the belly, a stem scar at one end and a blossom end at the other.
- About 700 seeds in a three-lobed ring at roughly two thirds of the radius (teardrops, wide end pointing outward), plus tiny air bubbles. Mesh seeds only near cut faces; a seed the knife goes through is kept by one side and eased just under the new face, so it shows through a thin film of jelly.
- Three varieties: Crimson, Golden, Rosé.

PIECES AND CUTTING
- Every piece is the melon SDF clipped by the half-spaces of the cuts that made it, with the fresh edges rounded (smooth max). All pieces share the melon's original rest frame, so rind, pith, stripes and seeds stay exactly where they grew.
- Knife tool: the user draws a line across the melon. Read the stroke on top of what it crosses to get a vertical blade plane. For each piece the plane passes through, fit the piece's best rotation, carry the plane into rest space, and split the piece in two.
- Build the new pieces cooperatively (generators with a per-frame time budget) while a steel knife (brushed blade, wooden handle with rivets) lines up over the stroke and presses a groove into the jelly. Swap the new pieces in the moment the edge breaks through, carrying over the position and velocity of the flesh they came from, and let the blade wedge them apart as it sinks. Allow up to about 24 pieces and reject slivers.
- For each piece: a surface-nets render skin (evaluate only the blocks near the surface, one Newton step onto it), a hex lattice in the piece's principal frame with boundary nodes snapped onto the surface, and a fast barycentric embedding.

PHYSICS (XPBD on the CPU, fixed 60 Hz, 6 substeps)
- Cell-wise co-rotational shape matching (8-node cells, warm-started rotation, strain stiffening), tet volume constraints for near-incompressibility, rind firmer than flesh.
- Edge damping, plus damping of each piece's deformation relative to its rigid motion (never its fall or tumble), rolling resistance on the table, and sleep when calm.
- Piece-to-piece contact against each other's exact SDF in a best-fit frame; sleeping pieces act as walls. Floor contact with Coulomb friction.
- Hand tool: grab any piece and pull (soft patch attachment, with enough reach to drag pieces across a wide table). Scroll or a second finger twists while holding.

title: 7-bar Dribbble-style UI motion loop with morphing states
author: ultimaxbt
prompt:
<inputs>
Ask me for: 8 to 12 UI states the shape should turn into (e.g. button, loader, player, slider, toggle, tabs, chart, command palette, toast), a pure black-and-white palette or one accent color, and a royalty-free track around 120 BPM (e.g. from Mixkit, free for commercial use).
</inputs>

<direction>
Dribbble-level UI motion. One shape, no cuts: each state is the same element changing size, radius and color, while its content swaps with a quick blur. A cursor triggers every change through actual clicks and drags. Use a light warm-gray canvas, black-and-white components and one clean UI font (Geist). Springs throughout, with only a slight overshoot. Zoom the camera so each state fills the frame. Match the final frame to the first for a seamless loop.
Banned: bouncy easing, particle bursts, glows, gradients on UI chrome, inconsistent icon strokes, dead time, anything that feels like a template.
</direction>

<structure>
120 BPM, 7 bars, with an action on every beat.
Button → loader → check → dynamic island → music player with a play/pause morph → scrub the progress bar → it turns into a volume slider that stretches when dragged past max → a toggle switches on the beat → its knob becomes a liquid tab indicator → the tabs expand into a chart that draws itself, with a tooltip on hover → it folds into ⌘K → type to filter → enter → toast → back to the button.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML file, square 1440x1440. Compute every style from time inside seek(t): no CSS transitions, timers or state carried between frames.
2. Use closed-form step responses for springs. If a value changes target multiple times, add one spring for each change so it remains a pure function of time.
3. Give the tab indicator’s two edges separate springs, letting the leading edge stretch ahead of the trailing one. Use the same approach for the toggle knob.
4. Make drags direct: while the cursor is held down, calculate the value from its position. On release, spring back from that position.
5. Analyze the song with numpy to find the beat grid and begin on a downbeat. Position each UI sound using its measured peak.
6. Render with Playwright: 4 subframes per frame, blended with ffmpeg tmix for motion blur at 60fps.
7. Render one frame per beat before the full render. Fix anything off-grid, cramped or difficult to read.
</build>

<gotchas>
Don’t use will-change on anything the camera scales, or the text will look blurry. Text swapping inside a morphing container needs separate enter and exit timing to avoid overlap. Make the final frame identical to the first—including cursor position and speed—or the loop will stutter.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for the inputs, then show me the state list on the beat grid before writing any code.

Button → loader → check → dynamic island → music player with a play/pause morph → scrub the progress bar → it becomes a volume slider that stretches when dragged past max → a toggle flips on the beat → the knob becomes a liquid tab indicator → the tabs open into a chart that draws itself, with a tooltip on hover → it collapses into ⌘K → type to filter → enter → toast → back to the button.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML file, square 1440x1440. Every style is computed from time inside seek(t): no CSS transitions, no timers, no state carried between frames.
2. Springs are closed-form step responses. A value that changes target many times is the sum of one spring per change, so it stays a pure function of time.
3. The tab indicator's two edges ride different springs, so the leading edge stretches ahead of the trailing one. Same trick for the toggle knob.
4. Drags are direct manipulation: while the cursor is held, the value is computed from its position. On release it springs back from wherever it was.
5. Analyze the song with numpy for the beat grid and start on a downbeat. Place every UI sound by its measured peak.
6. Render with Playwright: 4 subframes per frame, blended with ffmpeg tmix for motion blur at 60fps.
7. Render one frame per beat before the full render. Fix anything off the grid, cramped or hard to read.
</build>

<gotchas>
Never put will-change on anything the camera scales or the text renders blurry. Text that swaps inside a morphing container needs its own enter and exit timing or it overlaps. Make the last frame identical to the first, cursor position and speed included, or the loop stutters.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for the inputs, then show me the state list on the beat grid before you write any code.
</start>

title: Interactive 3D gummy citrus slice with soft-body wobble
author: vib3coded
prompt:
Create a beautiful, interactive 3D gummy citrus slice using WebGPU. Deliver the complete experience in one standalone HTML file with embedded JavaScript and WGSL shaders.

This must be a real-time 3D simulation, not a video, image, or looping animation.

APPEARANCE

Create a thick, semicircular orange slice with translucent, juicy flesh, eight distinct segments, delicate internal membranes, tiny bubbles, a pale pith layer, and a soft orange rind.

Make it look like premium gummy candy: saturated color, glossy highlights, light passing through the flesh, convincing refraction, and soft contact shadows. Avoid excessive bloom, washed-out colors, or a hard plastic appearance.

Use a warm, light studio background and a clean editorial interface with generous whitespace. Add the large italic serif title “Citrus Jelly.” Keep controls compact and the slice clearly visible.

SOFT-BODY PHYSICS

The jelly feel is the most important part.

- Grab any part of the slice with a mouse or finger.
- Pull, lift, stretch, twist, and release it.
- Make deformation local: pulling one edge should stretch nearby flesh while the rest follows naturally.
- After release, the slice should wobble, overshoot, and gradually recover its original shape.
- Include gravity, inertia, damping, ground collisions, and soft bouncing.
- Preserve volume approximately and prevent the mesh from collapsing or turning inside out.
- Make the rind slightly firmer than the flesh.
- Internal segments, membranes, and bubbles must follow the deformation without floating outside the body.

Use a stable volumetric soft-body solver, such as a tetrahedral mesh with XPBD constraints. Do not imitate softness by scaling or rotating the entire object.

CONTROLS

Include three color presets: Orange, Lemon, and Ruby.

Add:
- Firmness slider.
- Internal damping slider.
- “Give it a nudge” button.
- Reset button.
- Quarter-speed checkbox.
- Show mesh checkbox.
- Pause/resume button.

Display small live readouts for mass, percentage of rest volume, and kinetic energy.

TECHNICAL REQUIREMENTS

Use genuine WebGPU rendering with WGSL shaders. Generate all geometry and visual details procedurally, without imported models or image files.

Keep simulation updates independent of rendering frame rate. Support desktop and touch devices. Show a clear fallback message if WebGPU is unavailable.

Test strong dragging, repeated releases, all controls, and narrow screens. Fix unstable physics, broken geometry, and visual artifacts before delivering the finished HTML.

The result should feel like a tiny, tactile candy experiment that is genuinely satisfying to play with.

title: Blender CAD-to-assembly animation with motion and sound
author: Ayu_AI_0912
prompt:
Blender と Python を使って、機械・乗り物の「CAD 図面」と「設計図から組み上がって動き出す動画」を一式つくってください。

【題材】〇〇（例：D51 形蒸気機関車、帆船、からくり時計、複葉機）
【舞台】〇〇（例：夕焼けの田園、雪の鉄橋、海原。空欄なら題材に似合うものを選んで先に一言伝える）
【動き出し方】〇〇（例：煙を吐いて走り出す、帆を張って進む、歯車が回って鐘が鳴る）
【最後のロゴ】ロゴ画像のパス（なければ「なし」）

■ 成果物
1. 2D 図面（DXF、ezdxf で作成、A2 図枠・表題欄つき・単位 mm）
   - 一般組立図（側面図・平面図）、正面・背面図、主要部品の詳細図の 3 枚。寸法つき
   - 実物の図面ではなく「外観イメージ」であることを特記事項に書く
   - プレビュー PNG を書き出して自分の目で確認し、文字の重なりやはみ出しを直す
   - 3D モデル（OBJ/STL）の書き出しは不要
2. 動画 MP4（1920×1080、24fps、約 20 秒 + ロゴ 3 秒、音つき）

■ 作り方の方針
- 寸法・部品・動く部分の計算は 1 つの Python モジュールにまとめ、図面と Blender の両方がそれを読む
- 一般組立図の平面図は、機械を実際に置く位置に描く。その 1 枚をそのまま動画の「青焼きの紙」にする
- 部品ごとに組み立ての順番と入り方を決める
  - 上から落ちて弾む：重い部品
  - 横から滑り込む：筒や箱
  - 倒れた状態から起き上がる：薄い板
- 動く部品は回転の中心を原点にする。クランクやロッドなどの連動は数式で位置を計算し、毎フレームにキーを打つ

■ 動画の流れ
1. 青い紙の上に、白い線で図面が描かれていく（真上から）
2. 図面の線が白く光るワイヤーとして立ち上がる
3. 部品が次々と収まって組み上がる（カメラは寄り）
4. 青焼きが消えて【舞台】が現れる（カメラは引いて全景へ）
5. 【動き出し方】のとおりに動き出す
6. 完成カットでタイトル（被写界深度でぼけないよう、タイトルの間は絞る）
7. 最後にロゴのエンドカード

■ 煙・蒸気の作り方（EEVEE でうまくいった方法）
- 煙は 1 塊ずつ球のオブジェクトにする。出た時刻の煙突の位置から流し、だんだん大きく薄くする
- 体積（Volume）は使わない。球の表面に、縁ほど透ける半透明の材質（正面ほど濃く、ノイズでもくもく）を付ける
- 石炭の煙は暗い灰色にする。逆光で透けさせすぎると空と同じ色になって見えなくなる
- 景色全体を包む霞の箱（体積）は、ほかの体積を打ち消すので使わない。霞は地面の材質側で距離に応じて付ける

■ 音
外部音源は使わず、numpy/scipy で合成する。映像の出来事に合わせて置く：
図面を描く音、部品が収まるたびの金属音（重さで音色を変える）、景色の環境音、動き出しの音
（機関車ならブラスト音を車輪の回転に同期させる、汽笛、レールの継ぎ目）、懐かしい旋律。

■ 進め方
- 本番の前にテスト静止画（半分のサイズで 8〜10 枚）を描いて自分で確認し、直してから本番
- 本番レンダリングは、始める前に所要時間を伝えて了承を取る
  - PC に負荷をかけすぎないよう、区切りごとに休ませながら描く（EEVEE、サンプル数は控えめ）
- 完成したら MP4 の長さと映像・音声を確認し、数秒おきのコマを並べて見てから渡す
- 最後に、図面の中身・動画の流れ・音の要点を短く報告する

title: Interactive jelly crocodile simulation in three.js
author: vib3coded
prompt:
Build a single-file interactive three.js (r170, ES module via import map) soft-body study called "Crocodile Jelly" — No. 069 in a "Material Studies" series. A life-size crocodile cast in two layers of jelly lies on its belly on a pale studio table, legs splayed, mouth open.

Geometry (signed distance field, rest pose):
- Body: a flattened, boxy superellipse section swept along a gently curving Catmull–Rom spine from the tail tip to the snout. The tail is tall and narrow, the body broad and low, then a neck, a flat skull and a long flat snout ending in a rounded nose bulb. The belly is pressed into the table so the footprint is flat.
- Legs: four short, stocky legs built from tapered capsules (shoulder/hip → elbow/knee → wrist), splayed out sideways. Feet are flat on the table; the front feet have 5 spread toes, the hind feet 4.
- Tail crest: a double row of upright triangular plates that merges into a single row toward the tip.
- Back: rows of keeled scutes down the back, with a bigger pair on the nape. Eyes sit on raised bumps on top of the skull.
- Jaws: the mouth line sits a little below the middle of the head, so the lower jaw is a solid bar about a third of the head's depth. The upper head is built swung up about the corner of the mouth (about 17° open); the lower jaw lies flat and still on the table. The floor of the mouth is nearly flat and filled by a soft tongue pad; the palate is a shallow hollow.
- Teeth: one row of 13 sugar cones along each jaw edge, upper pointing down and lower pointing up, staggered so they interleave, every fourth one larger.
- Inside: about 22 small trapped air bubbles in the body, and 6 stomach slots down the middle for swallowed food.

Simulation:
- Hex lattice with 5 tets per cell, boundary nodes snapped to the surface and a node layer exactly on the floor.
- CPU XPBD shape matching on a fixed 60 Hz step with 10 substeps. Legs, crest and head are set firmer than the body.
- Render meshes from surface nets (clear jelly plus a cream core layer), embedded barycentrically in the tets.
- Two muscles made by rewriting rest shapes:
  (1) the head swings down about the corner of the mouth onto the still lower jaw. It breathes slowly half-open, opens wide when food approaches, and on "Snap" opens wide, slams shut and lunges forward;
  (2) a travelling-wave plus steady-turn bend of the spine. The tail sways lazily and the head turns toward the pointer; "Thrash" sends a hard wave down the body.

Rendering (hand-written ShaderMaterials):
- Key-light shadow map, a back-face thickness pass, and refraction through the front faces with Beer–Lambert absorption and a scattering tint.
- The cream layer fills the belly up to a scalloped line low on the flank and rises at the head to just under the mouth line, so the whole lower jaw is solid cream. It carries square belly plates.
- Clear jelly carries procedural scales in body coordinates (arc length × distance round the section): oblong plates in rows on the back and tail

title: Chrome extension spider crawler that summarizes webpage text live
author: AnatoliKopadze
prompt:
Build a Chrome extension (Manifest V3) called "TL;DR Crawler" that works on any normal web page.

WHAT IT DOES
Click the toolbar icon: a line-drawn spider appears on the current page, follows your cursor (also while scrolling), reads the text it walks over and builds a short TL;DR in a floating panel. Click the icon again: everything disappears and the page is exactly as before.

1. TOGGLE
- background.js: chrome.action.onClicked injects content.js with chrome.scripting.executeScript.
- content.js checks a global flag. If the crawler is already running, it shuts down and cleans up. Otherwise it starts. Only one instance per tab, ever.

2. FIND THE TEXT
- Find the main readable area: prefer <article> or <main>, otherwise the element with the most paragraph text. Skip nav, header, footer, aside, menus, forms, code, ads and hidden elements.
- Collect text blocks (p, li, blockquote, h2-h4) and split them into sentences. Store each sentence as a DOM Range (sentences can span links and bold text, so do NOT wrap them in elements).
- Watch the area with a debounced MutationObserver (1s) to pick up text loaded later (infinite scroll, lazy content).

3. PICK KEY SENTENCES
- Score each sentence: +2 digits, +2 for %, $, €, million, billion; +1.5 for words like first, record, launch, announce, new, only, biggest, fastest, warns, raises, cuts; +0.3 per capitalized name (max +2); -2 if under 40 or over 260 characters.
- Mark the top 25% as key sentences (min 5, max 80), spread so most paragraphs get one.
- Summaries, max 9 words each:
  - If an API key is set: send all key sentences in ONE request to Claude and ask for a JSON array of short, plain summaries (max 9 words, keep numbers and names exactly, no hype). Request again in batches when new text appears.
  - Without a key: fallback summary = the sentence with filler openers removed (and, but, however, also, according to), cut at a word boundary with "…".

4. THE SPIDER
- Shadow DOM host at document root containing a full-screen fixed <canvas> (pointer-events: none, z-index 2147483646) and the panel.
- Look: small rounded-rectangle body, abdomen ellipse, head with two white eyes, outlines in #5ab8ff. 8 legs as 3px blue lines with pink (#ff4f7a) joint dots, two segments each with inverse kinematics, knees bending outward.
- Gait: two alternating leg groups. A foot steps only when it's ~80px from its ideal spot and the other group is planted. Steps last 0.13s with a small lift, landing slightly ahead in the walking direction.
- Movement: target = cursor position + scroll, so it follows while scrolling. Max ~420 px/s, smooth acceleration, stops ~40px from the cursor, turns smoothly toward its direction. If the cursor is idle for 8s, it wanders around the viewport.
- requestAnimationFrame with a fixed 1/120s physics step. Support devicePixelRatio and window resize.

5. CRAWLING
- Every 80ms and on every foot landing, find the text under the spider with document.caretRangeFromPoint (ignore the extension's own elements).
- If that point is inside a key sentence not yet found: highlight it with the CSS Custom Highlight API (::highlight(tldr-found) with a soft yellow background) and add its summary to the panel.
- If a foot lands on a normal word: in ~25% of cases glitch just that word. Wrap only that word in a span (it's a single text node, so it's safe) and apply one random effect: monospace font, blue outline, blue highlight, slight rotation, wide letter-spacing, blur or uppercase. Max 2 effects per word. Record every change so it can be undone.

6. PANEL
- Top-right, draggable by its header, inside the Shadow DOM so site CSS can't affect it.
- Dark (#16181c), mono title "TL;DR" in yellow (#ffd166), a "found / total" counter, a pink progress bar and a numbered list in article order. The newest item flashes yellow and the list auto-scrolls to it. The list scrolls inside a max height.
- Buttons: "Copy TL;DR" (plain text to the clipboard), "Restart" (clears highlights, glitches and the list) and "Close" (full shutdown).
- If a key is set, add "Write TL;DR with Claude": sends all found sentences and returns 3 short lines using only their facts, numbers unchanged. Show a "Thinking..." state, then the answer under the list.

7. API KEY
- options.html: a field for the user's Anthropic API key and a model name, stored in https://t.co/YDJaSAQOTq.local.
- All API calls go through background.js with fetch to https://t.co/ePcSurB2Zg, with headers x-api-key, anthropic-version: 2023-06-01 and content-type: application/json.

title: House rebuilt in Blender from listing photos
author: noclipepe
prompt:
Reconstruct this entire property as a detailed 3D scene in Blender using only the attached real-estate listing photos as reference.
Treat all of the images as evidence of the same physical house. Study them together and infer one coherent floor plan, room layout, dimensions, floor levels, wall positions, openings, roof structure and connections between spaces.
Recreate as much of the property as can reasonably be inferred from the photos:
- full exterior architecture
- all visible interior rooms
- windows, doors and stairs
- kitchen cabinetry and appliances
- bathrooms and permanent fixtures
- fireplaces, trim and architectural details
- furniture and staging visible in the references
- driveway, lawn, landscaping, patio and surrounding context
- neighboring structures or environmental elements where they are visible
Accuracy to the references is the priority.
Do not create separate disconnected scenes for each photograph. Everything should belong to one consistent 3D house that still makes sense when viewed from angles that were not directly photographed.
Where dimensions or hidden geometry cannot be known exactly, infer them conservatively from the available views and normal architectural relationships. Avoid inventing unnecessary details.
Use real 3D geometry for the architecture and major scene elements. Do not fake the result by projecting the listing photos onto flat planes.
Match virtual cameras to the original photographs wherever possible. Use the reference images to continuously validate:
- overall silhouette
- wall and room proportions
- window and door placement
- roof geometry
- ceiling and floor heights
- room connections
- furniture scale
- important visual landmarks
Compare renders against the source photos during development and correct the geometry whenever several views disagree.
Use physically plausible materials, realistic scale, lighting and vegetation. Preserve the visual character of the original property rather than redesigning it.
Once the reconstruction is complete, create a polished continuous cinematic walkthrough that moves naturally through the exterior and interior of the house and clearly shows the reconstructed property.
The final result should feel like the viewer is walking through the same house shown in the listing photos.
Deliverables:
1. Complete Blender scene
2. Reproducible source/code used to build the scene
3. Cameras corresponding to the important reference photos
4. High-quality still renders for comparison with the originals
5. A finished cinematic walkthrough video

title: Offshore jelly cube diorama comparison
author: vib3coded
prompt:
Build "Offshore Jelly" — a single-file interactive WebGPU diorama in the "Material Studies" series: a stretch of North Sea cut out as a cube of translucent jelly, sitting on a studio floor. Everything is procedural (no external assets, no network), one HTML file with inline JS/WGSL.

THE BLOCK
- A wobbly jelly cube you can grab by its sides and tip; it springs back. Sliders: firmness, damping, wind (0–20 m/s).
- Inside: a shallow-water simulation for the sea surface (waves, wakes, foam, whitecaps), seabed with sand ripples, scour rocks, kelp, boulders, starfish, crabs, urchins, a pipeline, cables and a small wreck. Caustics on the seabed. Dragging the water stirs up waves.
- Waves come from the wind: several wave trains whose height grows with wind speed.

THE SCENE
- A production platform on a four-legged steel jacket (braces, risers, conductors, boat landing, marine growth below the waterline): main and cellar decks, process module, derrick, living quarters, lifeboats, a pedestal crane with a laydown area, a flare boom with a flickering flame and smoke.
- An octagonal helideck with an H, a net, perimeter lights and a windsock.
- Five offshore wind turbines on monopiles: transition piece with yellow platform, boat landing ladder, davit, tower, nacelle, three-blade rotors with red tips, blinking red aviation lights. Rotor speed and power output (MW) follow the wind.
- A rocky skerry with a lighthouse whose beam turns; seals haul out on it.

WHAT HAPPENS
- Supply run: a platform supply vessel comes in from standby, holds station next to the jacket on dynamic positioning (thruster foam), and the crane does four lifts — containers swing on the hook, are set down on the platform and back-loaded onto the boat's deck. Then she sails back to standby.
- Helicopter: flies in from the west, turns into the wind, lands on the helideck; a deck officer walks out; passengers get off. A second press sends it away (spin-up, lift, outbound). Rotor and tail rotor spin, downwash flattens the water.
- Crew boat: a small catamaran sails out to a turbine, pushes its bow onto the boat landing, and technicians climb the ladder onto the platform. Next time she picks them up and brings them home.
- Storm: the wind builds to a gale, waves get big with whitecaps and spray, rain falls, the room darkens, lightning strikes blades, the lighthouse, the derrick or the sea with a flash and thunder. Above cut-out the turbines feather their blades and stop (0 MW); the helicopter is grounded. Then it eases and the turbines restart.

LIFE
- Schools of fish around the jacket and wrecks, gulls that perch on railings and take off on the horn, gannets that plunge-dive for fish, a pod of porpoises, seals, moon jellyfish, crew walking the decks.

CONTROLS & UI
- Buttons: Supply run, Helicopter (take-off when landed), Crew boat, Storm. Space = ship's horn. Tapping a turbine switches it on/off, tapping the supply boat or helideck calls them. Orbit by drag, zoom by wheel/pinch.
- Tallies: Power (MW), Lifts, Flights; status lines for the supply boat, helicopter and crew boat.
- Flavours (jelly colour palettes): North Sea, Curaçao, Blackcurrant.
- Sounds are synthesised with WebAudio and only play for events (horn, winch, set-down, bump, rotor, thunder, rain) — no constant background ambience. Sound toggle and pause.
- Mobile: a bottom sheet with the controls, touch orbit and pinch zoom. Clean fallback message when WebGPU is unavailable.
- Copy in English: "Offshore Jelly. A wind farm and a platform working a stretch of North Sea, set in a block of jelly." — "Call in the supply boat. Fly the crew out. Brew up a storm."

title: Pixel-art 3D football yard simulation with kids and dog
author: N1njaCodex
prompt:
Build a single-page web toy called "Yard Box": a real-time 3D scene rendered as pixel art, showing a courtyard football box behind a four-storey panel apartment block on a floating island. Use three.js r160 (ES module via import map from jsDelivr, plus BufferGeometryUtils). English UI. Original design only — no real brands, places or logos.

RENDERING PIPELINE (the core look)
- Orthographic camera at an isometric angle (elevation ≈31°, azimuth π/4, rotatable in 90° steps with smooth easing; drag sideways or buttons to turn; wheel/pinch zoom 0.7–2.6).
- Render into a small WebGLRenderTarget (half-float, nearest filtering, depth texture) — about 480×300 art pixels at pixel size 3 — no anti-aliasing. Fit the island + the top of the block into the screen area left free by the UI, and snap the camera so the world origin lands on a whole art pixel (static things never shimmer).
- Post-pass ShaderMaterial: texelFetch whole-pixel upscale; depth-based outlines (a pixel > ~0.5 m in front of a neighbour darkens ×0.5); quantize every pixel to the nearest of a fixed ~60-colour palette in OKLab (lightness weighted ×1.35); optional 4×4 Bayer dither (off by default); empty depth = page background colour.
- "Raw 3D" toggle shows the full-resolution MSAA render without steps above. Controls: pixel size slider 2–6, palette / dither / outlines checkboxes.
- Palette: warm concrete greys, cool greys for snow in shade/moonlight, snow and sky blues, turf greens, autumn olives, yellows/oranges/rusts, team reds and blues, skin and wood tones, lamp/window yellows, dusk violets, mint for the boards.

LIGHT AND TIME
- Directional sun/moon with hard BasicShadowMap (2048), hemisphere fill, point lights for two streetlamps (decay 2) and weak doorway lamps. Presets Day / Dusk / Night blended over 1.6 s. Glow materials lerp between on/off colours.
- The block's facade uses an emissive map drawn on a canvas; at night windows glow warm or cool, and random flats switch lights on and off.

WORLD (all boxes, cylinders, extrusions; textures drawn texel by texel on canvases)
- Rounded floating slab: grass top over soil over rock.
- Football box: rounded-rectangle boards (22×12 m, mint green, plank lines, a gate with an open door), netting on posts above the boards at both ends, mini goals (3 m × 2 m) with alpha-tested nets, turf texture with mowing stripes, worn goalmouths/centre and white markings.
- Panel block along one long side: 4 floors, facade drawn panel by panel with windows and curtains, two entrances with canopies, random balconies, roof details; an asphalt strip with two benches and hedges.
- Dollhouse cut: when the camera looks from the block's side, hide the floors, roof, balconies and canopies and show a section of the ground floor instead — low cut walls with a dark cap, rooms with coloured floors, rugs, sofas, tables, wardrobes, TVs (glowing at night), pot plants, stairwells with steps and post boxes; room floors glow warm at night.
- Playground (swing that actually swings, slide, sandbox), birches with white trunks and dark marks, painted-tyre flower beds, a parked car, a washing line with swaying sheets, two lamp posts.

PEOPLE AND DOG
- Kids as rigs of ~17 boxes (bigger heads), posed every frame with two-bone IK: running stride, kicks keyed as back-swing → strike → follow-through, keeper stance, sideways dives, catch/hold/throw, goal celebrations (airplane arms).
- Three grandmothers sitting on the benches (cheer on goals), a small kid on the swing.
- A box-built dog that lives by the benches.

GAME LOGIC
- 3v3: two field players + one keeper per team (RED attacks +x, BLUE −x), first to 5, then a new game; scoreboard with score, game number, status line and games won.
- Kick-off from the centre; open play with dribbling by small touches, passes leading the receiver, shots aimed inside a post at random height with angular error growing with distance and pressure, tackles; players get behind the ball before kicking (feed-forward on a rolling ball), squeeze in at an angle when the ball is against the boards, avoid goal frames; a scramble poke if nobody can reach a still ball for 3.5 s.
- Keepers hold position, come out for slow loose balls, read shots after a 0.1–0.3 s reaction delay with some error, dive, catch or parry.
- Ball physics in 4 substeps: gravity, ground bounce (lower in winter), boards (lively below rail height, dead in the netting above), posts and crossbar, the goal net, legs in the way. Status flashes: GOAL!, SAVED!, WHAT A SAVE!, OFF THE POST!, OFF THE BOARDS, TACKLE.
- Every 100–170 s (or on a button) the dog runs in through the gate, grabs the ball, runs loops away from the kids for ~5 s, drops it and trots home; it gives up if the game resets.

SEASONS (Summer / Autumn / Winter)
- Summer: poplar fluff drifting. Autumn: yellow/orange canopies, leaves falling from the birches, leaf litter on the ground, olive grass. Winter: snow on the ground, roofs, benches, car and boards; bare trees; falling snow and kicked-up snow spray; kids wear hats; the ball turns orange.

INPUT AND UI
- Click the player on the ball to shoot, his teammate to pass, the pitch to make him dribble there; keys S, P, D, Space, Q/E or arrows.
- Layout: title and caption top-left, lit pixel-font scoreboard top-centre, a narrow control rail on the right (Time, Season, Game, View), a hint bottom-left, a fold-out "How it's drawn" panel bottom-right. Fonts: Silkscreen, Rubik, JetBrains Mono. Light and dark themes via CSS tokens; on phones everything stacks under the scene. WebGL2 fallback card.

title: Cozy Café Fluid Studio: interactive coffee and milk simulation
author: genevieve__h
prompt:
# Role & Objective
Act as a Principal Graphics Engineer and Creative Technologist specializing in Three.js, WebGL2/WebGPU, 3D Volumetric Fluid Dynamics, and GLSL Raymarching. 

Build a browser-based, photorealistic, interactive 3D coffee & milk physics sandbox ("Cozy Café Fluid Studio") designed to look like a viral macro-lens video on X. The user can orbit the camera freely (from 90° top-down to a 0° macro side-profile view), swap custom 3D glass vessels and ice cube shapes (with procedural fallbacks and a `.glb`/`.gltf` loader for Blender assets), and pour either Espresso or Heavy Cream directly from their cursor in any order.

---

# 1. Core Visual & Physics Architecture (True 3D Volumetric Fluid)
Because the camera can view the glass from the side, top, or any oblique angle, implement a **3D Eulerian Grid Fluid Solver** (e.g., `64x96x64` or `96x128x96` tiled 2D texture atlas or WebGL2 `sampler3D` / WebGPU 3D Storage Textures) confined to the bounding volume of the active glass mesh:

1. **Two-Fluid Miscible Density & Filling System:**
   - Track two separate scalar volume fields inside the glass: $\rho_{\text{coffee}}$ (dark absorbing fluid) and $\rho_{\text{milk}}$ (bright scattering fluid), plus a dynamic **Liquid Fill Height (
$h
_{\text{fill}}$)** that rises smoothly as the user pours either liquid into the glass.
   - Allow pouring in **any order**:
     - *Coffee first, then Milk:* Pouring espresso fills the glass with dark amber-black liquid and generates a thin golden crema foam layer on the top meniscus ($y \approx h_{\text{fill}}$). Pouring cold milk next shoots a dense white plume downward that billows back up via buoyancy.
     - *Milk first, then Coffee (Dirty Latte / Macchiato style):* Pouring cold milk fills the glass with opaque ivory liquid. Pouring hot espresso on top creates dark mahogany plumes that sink through the dense milk and stratify into layered gradients around the ice.

2. **Rayleigh-Taylor & Kelvin-Helmholtz Instabilities:**
   - Implement **MacCormack (or BFECC) Advection** so thin caramel ribbons do not smear out due to numerical dissipation.
   - Inject **Baroclinic Vorticity** ($\nabla \rho \times \nabla P$) and **Vorticity Confinement** ($\epsilon (\mathbf{N} \times \boldsymbol{\omega})$) along the interface between milk and coffee so sinking/rising plumes roll up into hyper-detailed mushroom caps and curling tendrils.

3. **3D Volumetric Raymarching Shader (Beer-Lambert + Multiple Scattering Approximation):**
   - Render the fluid volume inside the glass by raymarching through the 3D density texture (`sampler3D`).
   - **Optical Physics:** Do NOT use simple RGB `mix()`. Compute physically based **Beer-Lambert Law extinction** ($\sigma_a(\lambda) = \text{vec3}(1.6, 5.4, 13.5)$ for espresso so thin edges glow ruby/caramel-amber while thick regions are pitch black) combined with **isotropic + forward Henyey-Greenstein phase function scattering** for the milk fat globules (high albedo ivory-white).
   - Add a **Dual-Lobe Subsurface Scattering (SSS)** look by sampling a lower-MIP (blurred) level of the milk density volume for ambient internal light transport, creating a soft, milky amber glow where coffee and cream meet.

---

# 2. Custom Blender Assets (Glasses & Ice) + Procedural SDF Dual-Representation
Support loading custom Blender `.glb` meshes via `GLTFLoader` while providing built-in procedural geometries (and matching Signed Distance Fields) so the app runs out-of-the-box:

1. **Glass Shapes (Vessel Selector):**
   - **Fluted Café Glass:** Ribbed vertical ridges that distort and refract the swirling fluid inside.
   - **Double-Walled Borosilicate Mug:** Suspended inner rounded chamber showing floating liquid in mid-air.
   - **Stemless Wine / Tulip Glass:** Curved tapered bowl that forces sinking milk plumes inward toward the center.
   - **Classic Rocks Tumbler:** Heavy thick crystal base with sharp vertical walls.
   - *Rendering:* Use Three.js `MeshPhysicalMaterial` with `transmission: 0.98`, `ior: 1.52`, `thickness`, dispersion/chromatic aberration, and crisp studio softbox environment reflections.
   - *Physics Boundary:* Enforce a strict no-slip/no-penetration boundary condition against the inner wall SDF of the selected glass so fluid hugs the exact contour of the vessel.

2. **Ice Cube Shapes (Ice Selector):**
   - **Large Craft Sphere:** A single giant crystal-clear sphere in the center that splits the pour stream into a ring vortex.
   - **Beveled Bistro Cubes (x3):** Stacked at angles inside the glass, creating narrow channels for cream tendrils to snake through.
   - **Hollow Cylinder / Bullet Ice:** Allows fluid to pour through the center hole and billow out the bottom.
   - **Crushed / Pebble Ice:** A porous top cluster that diffuses the pour into dozens of tiny trickling caramel fingers.
   - *Rendering & Physics:* Render ice with `ior: 1.31`, internal frost fracture planes, and real-time refraction of the raymarched fluid behind it. Stamp the ice SDFs into the 3D fluid solver's obstacle buffer so plumes physically collide with, wrap around, and slide underneath the ice cubes. Include buoyant bobbing when liquid height rises.

---

# 3. Interactive Pouring & Camera Controls
1. **Cursor-Driven Pour Stream:**
   - Raycast the mouse cursor onto a horizontal plane above the glass rim.
   - **Left-Click & Hold:** Pour a visible, glossy 3D parabolic liquid stream (rendered as a dynamic tube mesh or raymarched metaball stream) from the cursor into the glass.
   - **Mouse Speed & Scroll Wheel:** Moving the mouse whips the stream across the surface; scrolling adjusts **Pour Height / Velocity** (a high pour punches deep to the bottom of the glass with high turbulence; a low pour gently floats layers on the surface).
2. **Seamless Orbit Camera (`OrbitControls`):**
   - Right-click drag (or two-finger drag) smoothly orbits from **Macro Side View** (watching plumes dive down the glass wall) to **Top-Down Latte Art View** (watching crema swirl around the ice).
   - Include quick camera preset buttons: `[Side Profile]`, `[45° Café Angle]`, and `[Top-Down Macro]`.

---

# 4. Minimalist Cozy UI & Atmosphere
- **Environment:** A warm, sunlit wooden tabletop with soft morning window blinds casting subtle gobos/caustics, warm beige/linen background tones, and a shallow depth-of-field (`BokehPass`) on the background.
- **Minimalist Floating Dock (Bottom Center, frosted glass `backdrop-filter: blur(12px)`, rounded pill buttons, warm serif/sans typography):**
  - **Liquid Toggle:** `[ ☕ Pour Espresso ]` | `[ 🥛 Pour Heavy Cream ]`
  - **Vessel Picker:** `[ Fluted ]` `[ Rocks ]` `[ Tulip ]` `[ Double-Wall ]` `[ + Load .GLB ]`
  - **Ice Picker:** `[ Sphere ]` `[ Bistro Cubes ]` `[ Crushed ]` `[ None ]`
  - **Simulation Controls:** `Pour Speed` slider, `Time Scale` slider (`0.1x Slow-Mo` to `1.0x`), `[ Stir with Glass Straw ]` tool, and `[ Empty Glass ]` reset button.

---

# Deliverable Instructions
Provide a complete, runnable HTML/JS/GLSL implementation (or clean modular Vite + Three.js setup) with zero missing placeholders. Prioritize the 3D raymarched Beer-Lambert coffee/milk shader, the 3D fluid advection/vorticity compute passes, and the refractive glass/ice boundary coupling so it runs at 60fps.

title: Cinematic medieval catapult siege scene with flaming projectile
author: Lummox_eth
prompt:
10-second cinematic video, square 1:1, one continuous shot, real-time action.

A large medieval wooden mangonel catapult rolls briskly from left to right along a muddy grassy ridge. Its four wheels rotate visibly, bouncing over uneven ground and throwing up dust. The machine has a sturdy timber chassis, iron fittings, tensioned ropes, and one long pivoting throwing arm ending in an open spoon. A single burning stone rests inside the spoon.

WIDE SIDE TRACKING SHOT. Keep the complete catapult visible throughout its full range of motion: all wheels, chassis, and the spoon at its highest position. The entire machine with its fully raised arm fits within the central 70 percent of the frame. Leave clear space above the raised spoon and ahead of the moving chassis. Maintain a constant camera distance with a subtle tracking arc. No zoom-in, no cuts.

0–3 seconds: the catapult is already rolling from the first frame. Its throwing arm is cocked backward, carrying the burning stone. Wheels rattle, ropes vibrate, grass bends, and dust trails behind.

3–5 seconds: the throwing arm snaps upward through a strong, clearly visible arc. The burning stone physically separates from the spoon and flies forward toward a distant castle. The empty spoon remains attached to the arm. The chassis jolts backward from recoil, and its wheels briefly bounce before settling.

5–8 seconds: the catapult continues rolling while the projectile follows a high ballistic arc across the sky, trailing flame, sparks, and smoke. Keep the catapult as the main subject.

8–10 seconds: the projectile strikes the distant castle wall, producing a brief burst of fire, stone fragments, and spreading dust. The intact catapult remains fully visible in the foreground, its empty arm settling after the throw.

Premium photoreal historical film VFX. Detailed weathered timber, worn iron, coarse ropes, realistic weight and mechanical motion. A spectacular mountain valley surrounds the ridge, with a medieval stone castle on a distant cliff. Golden sunset backlight, dramatic clouds, atmospheric depth, windblown grass, and rich natural colors.

The projectile is thrown by the swinging spoon, with no barrel or muzzle blast. One machine, one throwing arm, one projectile. No text, logos, interface, or split screen.

Sound: heavy wooden wheels rattling over dirt, creaking timber, tightening ropes, a sharp mechanical THWACK at release, a fiery projectile whoosh, and a distant stone impact. Continuous wind underneath. No music or speech.

title: Interactive gummy bear physics demo in a single HTML file
author: MiaAI_lab
prompt:
Build "Gummy Bears" - a single self-contained HTML file (three.js from a CDN is the only dependency): a handful of translucent gummy bears on a white table that you can grab, stretch, squash, throw and pour.

The bears

- Classic gummy bear silhouette: round head with two ears, short snout, plump body, stubby arms and legs, tiny molded eyes and nose - Every part melts smoothly into the next - build the body as an implicit surface (metaballs / marching cubes), not separate spheres - Material: real gummy candy. Translucent with transmission and refraction, colored light absorption that gets deeper in thick parts, glossy clearcoat with sharp highlights - Colors: cherry red, orange, lemon yellow, apple green, clear pineapple - Soft colored shadow under each bear, tinted by the bear's own color

Physics (this is the whole point - it must feel like jelly, not plastic)

- Each bear is a soft body: mass points for head, ears, snout, body, belly, hands and feet, held together by volume-preserving shape matching

- Limbs and neck are rendered as stretchy strands between points, getting thinner as they stretch

- Grab any part and pull: it stretches like rubber, the rest of the bear leans after it, on release it snaps back with a damped wobble

- Pull the head up: the neck stretches, the body follows, on release the bear squashes and hops

- Press down on the head: the bear pancakes, bulges sideways, then launches itself back up

- Throw a bear: it flies, squashes on landing, bounces and pushes other bears out of the way

- Bears collide with each other and never pass through one another

- Idle bears do small random hops with squash and stretch

- "Pour more bears" drops a handful from above into a wobbling, jiggling pile

UI

- Editorial product-page style on a white background. Large italic serif title "Gummy / Bears.", a short subtitle, a minimal card on the right with flavor swatches, a wobble slider, live "Stretch" and "Bounces" readouts and a "Pour more bears" button

- A subtle circular cursor that grows while grabbing

- ACES tone mapping, environment reflections, soft key and back light. Smooth 60fps

title: PRD — Police Chase Arcade Game Working title: Heatwave Platform: iOS…
author: froessell
prompt:
PRD — Police Chase Arcade Game

Working title: Heatwave
Platform: iOS + Android
Engine: Unity
Genre: Top-down 3D arcade chase / survival
Orientation: Portrait
Input: One-thumb touch controls
Business model: TBD — design MVP around gameplay first
Primary goal: Build a genuinely fun playable prototype before adding progression or monetization.
⸻
Product vision
A fast, chaotic mobile arcade game where the player is constantly being pursued by increasingly aggressive police.
The player cannot directly attack.
Instead, they survive by driving aggressively, drifting around obstacles, making sudden turns and tricking pursuing police into crashing into obstacles and each other.
The fantasy is:
You’re not stronger than the police. You’re harder to catch.

Runs should produce constant near-misses, chain collisions and moments where the player escapes a seemingly impossible situation.

Think:

easy controls + aggressive pursuit + physics chaos + escalating pressure.

⸻

Core gameplay loop

START RUN
↓
DRIVE / DRIFT
↓
POLICE PURSUE
↓
BAIT POLICE
↓
DODGE
↓
POLICE CRASH
↓
GAIN SCORE
↓
WANTED LEVEL INCREASES
↓
MORE / HARDER POLICE
↓
SURVIVE
↓
EVENTUALLY GET CAUGHT
↓
SCORE / RESTART

Target run duration:

2–5 minutes.

Restart should take less than 2 seconds.

⸻

Design principles

3.1 One-thumb playable

The player should be able to understand the controls within seconds.
No accelerator.
No brake pedal.
No virtual steering wheel.
The vehicle moves automatically.
The player controls only direction.

(I moved away from this after testing it the first time and added the onscreen joystick)

3.2 Arcade physics, not simulation
Vehicles should:
drift
slide
bounce
spin
collide dramatically
recover quickly
Fun takes priority over physical accuracy.

3.3 Pursuers are weapons
Police are effectively the player’s offensive mechanic.
The player should learn:
“If I turn here, that cop is going straight into that wall.”
3.4 Chaos should remain readable

Even with 10+ vehicles on screen, the player must immediately understand:
where they are
where they’re moving

where police are coming from

what can kill them

3.5 Failure should feel fair

Death should generally result from a mistake the player understands rather than unpredictable physics.

⸻

MVP scope

Do not build progression, upgrades, missions or monetization for the first milestone.

The first version contains:

1 player vehicle

1 arena

1 police vehicle

1 elite police variant

5 wanted levels

physics collisions

environmental obstacles
scoring
player health
police destruction
basic VFX
basic audio

game-over screen

instant restart

That’s enough to determine whether the game deserves further development.

⸻

Player vehicle

Movement

Player vehicle uses a Rigidbody-based arcade controller.

Do not rely heavily on realistic WheelColliders.
Core variables should be exposed in the Unity Inspector:
Acceleration
Maximum Speed
Turn Speed
Turn Curve
Lateral Grip
Drift Factor
Vehicle Mass
Collision Force
Drag
Angular Drag
Recovery Speed
These need to be extremely easy to tune.

⸻

Controls

Recommended first implementation:

Drag steering

Player touches anywhere on the lower portion of the screen.

Dragging horizontally controls steering.

← drag          turn left
→ drag          turn right
Vehicle accelerates automatically.
Steering should be relative rather than absolute.
The player should be able to lift their finger without immediately losing control.
Alternative to prototype
Test:
Hold left/right side of screen = steer left/right.
Don’t commit until both have been tested on a physical phone.
⸻
Drift system
Drifting should happen naturally when turning at speed.
No dedicated drift button.
At low speed:
high traction

At high speed:

reduced lateral traction

This produces controlled sliding.

Long drifts can optionally award score.

Example:

DRIFT
+120
LONG DRIFT
+340

But drift scoring is secondary to police destruction.

⸻
Police AI
Police should feel:
aggressive, predictable and slightly stupid.
They should not simply follow the player’s current position.
Instead, calculate an interception target based on player velocity.
Conceptually:
target =
playerPosition
+
playerVelocity * predictionTime
Police therefore try to cut the player off.
⸻
Police intelligence

Police intentionally have limited obstacle avoidance.

This is important.

Perfect navigation would make the game less fun.

Police should:

pursue aggressively

attempt interception

avoid obvious static obstacles

poorly account for other police
overshoot turns

collide with each other

occasionally take dangerous routes

This creates opportunities for the player.

⸻

Police destruction

Police can be destroyed by:

high-speed obstacle collisions

hitting another police vehicle

chain collisions

environmental hazards

The player does not have weapons.

Example scoring:

COP SMASHED
+250
DOUBLE SMASH
+600
TRIPLE SMASH
+1,000
PILEUP!
+2,000

Chain collisions should be heavily rewarded.

⸻

Wanted system

Wanted level controls difficulty.

★☆☆☆☆
★★☆☆☆
★★★☆☆
★★★★☆
★★★★★

Wanted level increases based primarily on survival time and score.
Level 1
2 police.
Slow and forgiving.

Level 2

3–4 police.

Slightly faster.

Level 3

5–6 police.

More aggressive interception.

Level 4

7–9 police.

Elite police introduced.
Level 5
Maximum chaos.
10+ police depending on device performance.

Elite units appear frequently.

The game should eventually become effectively impossible.

That’s intentional.

⸻

Elite police

The MVP only needs one special police type.

Interceptor

Visually distinct vehicle.
Characteristics:
faster than standard police
lower mass
aggressive prediction
sharp steering
easier to destroy in collisions

This creates a glass-cannon pursuer.

⸻

Player health

Use a simple health bar.

Example:
HULL
██████░░░░
Minor impacts:
small damage.

Heavy impacts:

large damage.

Extremely high-speed impacts:
potential instant destruction.
Police contact alone shouldn’t immediately kill the player.
This allows chaotic scrambles.
⸻
Arena
First arena should be compact.
Something roughly equivalent to:

ROCK

┌─────────────┐
│             │
│   ROCK      │
│             │
│       ███   │
│             │
│ ROCK        │
│         ROCK│
└─────────────┘

Obstacles need enough space between them for high-speed movement.

Avoid procedural generation initially.

Hand-design one good arena.
⸻
Environment
For the first visual theme, I’d use something other than water so we’re not cloning the reference too closely.
My preference:

Desert outlaw chase

Player is an outlaw escaping through a stylized desert environment.

Environment contains:

rock formations

cacti

barriers

abandoned vehicles

ramps

fences

small buildings

dust

destructible props

It also fits the chunky visual language you’re already exploring with Bolt Pit.

⸻

Camera

Top-down perspective camera.

Not completely vertical.

Something approximately:

55–70° downward angle.

Camera follows player with smoothing.

Camera should look slightly ahead in the player’s travel direction.

At high speed:

camera pulls back slightly.

At low speed:

camera moves closer.

⸻
Camera juice
Small camera effects make a large difference.
Light collision
Tiny shake.

Heavy collision

Strong short shake.

Police destruction

Shake + tiny freeze frame.

Example:

50–100 ms hit stop.
Large pileup

Slight zoom impulse + shake + particles.

Don’t overdo continuous shaking.

⸻

Visual style

Chunky stylized 3D.

Characteristics:

simplified geometry

exaggerated proportions

bright readable vehicles

soft lighting

minimal textures

strong silhouettes

exaggerated particles
Avoid realistic vehicle proportions.
Cars should feel almost toy-like.
⸻
VFX
Minimum MVP effects:
Player
dust trail
tire/skid marks
drift smoke

impact sparks

Police

siren lights

smoke when damaged

destruction explosion

debris

Environment

dust

destructible objects

impact particles

⸻
Collision feedback
Every significant collision should combine:
physics + particles + audio + camera response.
Major police destruction:
IMPACT
→ physics impulse
→ vehicle fragments/debris
→ sparks
→ smoke
→ camera shake
→ hit stop
→ sound
→ score popup
This interaction is one of the game’s main sources of satisfaction.
⸻
Score system

Score comes from:

ActionExample
Surviving+10/sec
Police destroyed+250
Driftvariable
Near miss+100
Double collision+600
Triple collision+1,000
Large pileup+2,000

Exact values should remain configurable.

⸻

Near misses

Optional for MVP but potentially valuable.

Detect when a police vehicle passes extremely close to the player at high relative velocity.

Display:

CLOSE CALL! +100

This rewards risky driving.

⸻

UI

During gameplay keep UI extremely minimal.

SCORE                          COINS
13,590                          14
★★★☆☆
WANTED
GAME
HULL
████████░░

No minimap initially.

Off-screen police can use subtle edge indicators.

⸻

Game over

When hull reaches zero:

brief slow motion.

Player crashes.

Then:

BUSTED
SCORE
24,850
BEST
31,220
[ AGAIN ]

Tapping anywhere could restart.

Avoid unnecessary menus between runs.

⸻

Audio

The soundscape should sell speed and collisions.

Required:

engine

tire squeal

police sirens
impact
metal crunch
debris
destruction
UI score sounds
wanted level increase

Sirens should become increasingly chaotic as wanted level increases.

⸻

Technical architecture

Suggested Unity structure:

GameManager
Player
├── PlayerController
├── VehiclePhysics
├── PlayerHealth
└── PlayerEffects
Police
├── PoliceController
├── PoliceAI
├── VehiclePhysics
├── PoliceHealth
└── PoliceEffects
Systems
├── SpawnManager
├── WantedManager
├── ScoreManager
├── AudioManager
├── CameraManager
└── PoolManager
UI
├── HUD
├── WantedUI
├── ScoreUI
├── HealthUI
└── GameOverUI

Avoid building an elaborate framework.

⸻
Object pooling
Police, particles and debris should use object pooling.
Avoid frequent:

Instantiate()
Destroy()

during gameplay.
Mobile performance should be considered from the beginning.
⸻
Performance target

Target:

60 FPS
on a mid-range modern iPhone/Android device.
Initial limits:

~12 active vehicles

~100 simple debris/particles

simple shadows

limited real-time lights

Performance should be tested on device early.

⸻
Development milestones
Milestone 1 — Greybox driving
Build:
empty arena
cube player
touch steering
acceleration
drifting

camera

Success criterion:

Driving around an empty arena feels satisfying.

Do not continue until it does.

⸻
Milestone 2 — The chase
Add:
one police vehicle
pursuit AI
interception
collisions
Success criterion:

Dodging one police car is entertaining.

⸻

Milestone 3 — Emergent chaos

Add:

multiple police

police-police collisions

obstacles

destruction

scoring

Success criterion:

Player can intentionally cause:

police → police
and
police → environment
collisions.
This is the critical milestone.
⸻
Milestone 4 — Escalation

Add:

wanted levels

spawning

difficulty scaling

interceptor

Now a run has an arc:

calm
↓
pressure
↓
chaos
↓
panic
↓
death

⸻

Milestone 5 — Juice
Add:
particles
camera shake
hit stop
skid marks

dust

sirens

collision sounds

score popups

⸻

Milestone 6 — Mobile build

Build for real devices.
Test:
controls
performance
readability
battery/thermal behaviour
different screen ratios
⸻
Milestone 7 — Decide whether to continue

At this point, stop development temporarily.

Don’t immediately build a garage and 37 unlockable cars.

Put the build in front of people.

The important questions are:

Do people immediately understand it?
Do they restart after dying?
Do they intentionally try to make cops crash?
Does “one more run” happen naturally?
If not, work on the core loop rather than adding content.
⸻
Phase 2 — only after validation
If the prototype works, then expand into:
Cars
↓
Coins
↓
Unlocks
↓
Challenges
↓
New arenas
↓
Special police
↓
Upgrades
↓
Daily challenges
↓
Leaderboards
Potential environments:
desert
city
docks
snow
industrial yard
airport
construction site
military base
And then there’s room for ridiculous police units: SUVs, armored vans, helicopters dropping roadblocks, etc.

I have opened a @[Unity CLI installation] project which we can work in. The art style of the game should be fun and cartoony and the action also over the top.
I have imported the Topdown engine into the project as well that we can use:
https://topdown-engine.moremountains.com/

I want the game to be optimized for mobile, but should work on desktop while testing.

title: Pixel-art 3D lido with diving meet, pools, and physics
author: vib3coded
prompt:
Build "Deep End": an open-air lido on a floating island of earth and rock, rendered as a real-time 3D scene in pixel art (three.js, orthographic isometric camera rendering into a small low-res target, no anti-aliasing, depth-buffer outlines, every pixel snapped to a fixed 64-colour palette matched in OKLab; quarter-turn rotation, zoom, pixel-size slider, Raw 3D toggle).
Scene: a 25 m lap pool and a 5 m deep diving pool cut into a concrete deck; 1 m and 3 m springboards that visibly bend; a 1930s concrete diving tower with platforms at 5, 7.5 and 10 m and an open stair; striped changing cabins with a clock, a kiosk, loungers and parasols; a judges' table.
Diving meet with real physics: each dive is flown, not animated — takeoff speed and angular momentum are solved to land the somersaults, angular momentum is conserved so tucking spins the diver faster and kicking out slows them to line up the entry. Divers kick out slightly early or late (more on harder dives), the entry angle sets the splash, five judges hold up score cards, highest and lowest are dropped, the rest are multiplied by the degree of difficulty. Events: 10 m, 3 m, free swim.
Water: each pool surface is a wave-equation height field (~20 cm cells) — entries, strokes, rain and clicks make rings that bounce off the walls; shaded from its normals with sun glints and a mirrored reflection of the lido; caustics on the tiled floor.
People: box-rig figures with two-bone IK — swimmers doing freestyle, breaststroke and backstroke with flip turns; divers swim to the ladder, shower, sit in the warm tub and climb again; children who run and get whistled at by the lifeguard; wet footprints on the deck that dry in the sun.
Light and weather: day / dusk / night (pool lights glow underwater, tower floodlights at night), dry / rain (rain rings the water and darkens the deck). Click the water to make a splash. Side panel with the meet scoreboard, controls and a short "How it's drawn" note. Original fictional content only, English UI.
